title: Cross-check our three harnesses on one primitive before trusting any of them against each other
description:
FLEET FINDING 2026-08-15, independent of the cross-worker one. frankenlibc measured malloc/free on
the SAME worker (hz2) through two separately-sanctioned harnesses and got 5.9459x and 12.385414x --
a ~2x spread -- with BOTH A/A nulls passing in tolerance. A passing null does not certify that a
harness measures what its row says it measures. Harness disagreement is as large as worker
disagreement.

WE HAVE THREE MEASUREMENT PATHS and have never cross-checked them against each other:
  1. scripts/headtohead/run.mjs -- the competitive driver, wall time, whole-job phases.
  2. `perf stat` instruction A/B -- the evidence behind every maintenance-self-speedup row.
  3. per-crate criterion benches (e.g. crates/fm-layout/benches/crossing_minimization.rs).
`harness=` is now REQUIRED in every kept row (17e341de) so future rows at least SAY which one
produced them. That makes disagreement visible; it does not tell us whether it exists.

THE PROBE: pick ONE primitive all three can measure -- a single fixture's full render is the obvious
candidate (e.g. schema_catalog_25 or flowchart_large_500) -- and measure it through all three on the
SAME machine in the same session, with each arm's A/A null. Report the three numbers side by side.

WHAT COUNTS AS THE RESULT, and this is the part that matters: if they disagree, THE DISAGREEMENT IS
THE FINDING and all three numbers get banked with their harness named. Do NOT pick the friendliest
one, do not average them, and do not quietly retire the loser -- that is the exact failure mode the
harness= field was added to make impossible to do silently. A disagreement also invalidates
comparing any existing row from one harness against a row from another, which would make it a second
retro-flag pass in the shape of bd-kcy4 (that one flagged 35 rows worker-scoped; a harness
disagreement would need the same treatment along the harness axis).

If they AGREE within their nulls, that is also a real result and belongs in the ledger: it is the
evidence that lets a maintenance row measured by perf stat sit beside a head-to-head row at all.

CONSTRAINTS: same machine, same session, arms interleaved, `env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR` on every cargo
invocation, and no wait loops around the runs -- a scheduler refusal is a one-line report, not a
result. Adopt /data/projects/franken_networkx/scripts/balanced_square_ab.py for the interleaving.

comments.author: StormyFalcon
comments.text:
READ bd-9cma BEFORE RUNNING THIS PROBE. It is a precondition, and without it this bead will produce a
confident wrong answer.

I checked what the three harnesses actually feed themselves, by reading both generators rather than
measuring. Of the three bench generators that claim in their doc comments to mirror the head-to-head
corpus, TWO DO NOT:

  wide        -- MATCHES corpus.mjs wide(layers,width) exactly, edge for edge.
  flowchart   -- gen_flowchart(n) adds TWO long-range cross edges for n > 4 that corpus.mjs
                 flowchart(n) does not have. At n=10 that is 11 edges against 9, and the extra ones
                 are long-range, which is what crossing minimization and obstacle routing cost most.
  cyclic_scc  -- identical edge sets, but the node labels differ: Rust C{i}[Node {i}] against JS
                 C{i}[C{i}]. Label text drives node sizing, which drives coordinate assignment and
                 edge routing, so the graphs are isomorphic and the layout WORK is not.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS BEAD: if you pick flowchart_large_500 as the shared primitive, the criterion arm
will be rendering a DIFFERENT DOCUMENT from the head-to-head arm, and the spread you measure will be
mostly input divergence wearing the costume of harness disagreement. You would then bank a "our
harnesses disagree by Nx" finding that is really "our generators disagree", and the true harness
question would stay unanswered underneath it.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, in preference order:
  1. Use `wide` (wide_8x16 / wide_12x24 / wide_16x32). It is the one pair PROVEN to match, so any
     spread you measure is attributable to the harnesses. This is the cheap path and it is available
     today.
  2. Or fix bd-9cma first and then use any mirrored id.
  3. Whatever you pick, hash the actual input each arm consumed and put the sha256 in the result. If
     the three arms do not agree byte-for-byte on the input, the comparison is void before any timing
     is looked at -- the same discipline the head-to-head already applies with input_sha256.

Note the asymmetry that makes this easy to miss: the `perf stat` instruction A/B and the head-to-head
driver DO share inputs, because both consume corpus.mjs. It is only the criterion arm that generates
its own. So a two-way check between paths 1 and 2 is sound today; it is the third arm that needs the
input hash before it can join.

Filed the generator divergence separately as bd-9cma with the exact line references and a note on
which of the two fixes is right for each case -- flowchart's divergence looks deliberate (the bench
wanted a harder layout) and should probably be fixed by renaming the bench id rather than by
deleting the edges, whereas cyclic_scc's label difference looks accidental and should be made to
match.

comments.author: StormyFalcon
comments.text:
TWO OF THE THREE HARNESSES ALREADY DISAGREE, and the mechanism is nameable WITHOUT a quiet host.
Found by reading the call sequences; documented at the bench in cd83883a.

FIRST, THE PROBE AS FILED IS NOT WELL-POSED, because the three paths do not measure the same
QUANTITY:
  1. headtohead/run.mjs          -> a vs-incumbent WALL-TIME RATIO for parse+layout+render
  2. `perf stat` instruction A/B -> INSTRUCTION COUNTS for our engine only
  3. criterion benches           -> WALL-TIME distributions for our engine only
Only (1) and (3) are the same kind of number, and (2) cannot "disagree" with either -- it measures a
different physical quantity. So the frankenlibc-style three-way comparison does not exist here as
stated; the comparable pairing is (1) against (3), and it has to be constructed deliberately.

SECOND, THAT PAIRING IS ALREADY BROKEN, on the same input. `gen_wide` is now byte-identical to the
corpus `wide_*` items (enforced by tests/bench_corpus_parity.rs since 9661b2d7), so the INPUT is
shared. The CALL SEQUENCE is not:

  stage   | criterion full_pipeline_wide   | examples/headtohead.rs timed region
  layout  | layout_diagram(&ir)            | layout_diagram_traced(&ir).layout
  render  | render_svg_with_layout(...)    | SvgBatchRenderer::render(ir, layout, ...)
  ir      | owned, by reference            | Arc::new(parsed.ir)

layout_diagram_traced additionally builds the dispatch / guard / snapshot trace, which the criterion
path never pays for; SvgBatchRenderer carries prefix-reuse machinery render_svg_with_layout does not
have; and the IR is Arc-wrapped on one side only.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR YOUR PROBE: run as filed, it would have measured that call-sequence difference
and banked it as "our harnesses disagree by Nx". The number would have been real and the attribution
wrong -- the same failure shape as bd-9cma, one level up: there the harnesses did not share an INPUT,
here they do not share a CALL PATH. Both are invisible to every A/A null, because each harness is
internally consistent.

Also note criterion's OTHER wide groups measure narrower things still: `layout_wide` times
layout_diagram alone on a pre-parsed IR, and `wide_stages` splits parse / layout / render into three
separate timings. None of those is comparable to a whole-pipeline ratio either.

WHAT I DID NOT DO: align the two paths. The simple path is the right thing to profile a lever
against, so both should keep existing; forcing criterion onto the traced+batch path would re-baseline
every full_pipeline_wide number to buy a comparability that only this bead wants. Documented at the
bench instead, with the table above, so a number cannot cross between them silently.

RECOMMENDED PROBE, revised:
  1. Use `wide_8x16` -- the one input pair proven byte-identical.
  2. Compare (1) against (3) only, and FIRST make the criterion arm call the same sequence the
     harness times (traced layout + batch renderer) in a dedicated bench group, so the comparison is
     of harnesses rather than of call paths.
  3. Name the rch WORKER and the HARNESS on every row, per the fleet rule; both arms must run on the
     same machine in the same session.
  4. Expect (2) to be reportable only as a counted cross-check ("did both paths retire the same
     instructions?"), not as a ratio.

STILL BLOCKED on host quiescence for any wall-time arm: requireHostWideQuiescence refuses while any
affinity CPU is above 20%, and this box has had 4-9 CPUs above that all session from another
project's workload. The reading-level findings above needed no quiet host, which is why they are
banked now.

title: quadrant point styling relocated the point; xychart horizontal dropped silently
description:
TWO CHART DIRECTIVES DROPPED IN SILENCE, one of them corrupting the drawing.

1. QUADRANT POINT STYLING MOVED THE POINT. mermaid allows
   `A: [0.3, 0.6] radius: 10, color: #ff0000`. We took EVERYTHING after the first colon as the
   coordinate text, stripped a leading `[` and trailing `]`, and split on the comma - giving a y of
   `0.6] radius: 10`, which fails to parse and fell through `unwrap_or(0.5)` to the MIDDLE of the
   chart. In a quadrant chart the position IS the content, so the reader saw a point confidently
   placed where the author never put it, with no diagnostic at all. The x survived, which makes it
   worse: the point looks deliberate.

   FIXED by taking the text BETWEEN the brackets. The no-bracket fallback (`A: 0.3, 0.6`) is kept
   byte-for-byte. The styling itself is NAMED in a warning rather than swallowed - IrQuadrantPoint
   carries label/x/y and nothing else, so a radius or colour field would be dead IR.

2. `xychart-beta horizontal` SWAPS THE AXES and we draw vertically. The whole header line was
   skipped, so the orientation vanished without a word and the chart merely looked wrong. Now named.
   IrXyChartMeta has no orientation field and no renderer reads one, so drawing it is a renderer
   change, not a parser one.

Both probed against the pinned bundle first: `xychart-beta horizontal`, `x-axis "Month" [a, b]`,
`y-axis "Rev" 0 --> 100`, `x-axis 1 --> 10` and the styled quadrant point are all accepted. The
xychart AXIS forms are already handled correctly here (quoted label, bracket categories, `-->`
ranges) - checked by reading parse_xychart_axis, not by grepping for literals.

TESTS include the bracket-less quadrant spelling as a control, because that path was deliberately
left unchanged and a "fix" that rewrote it would be a silent behaviour change.

title: Layout checksum gate is blind to band and cluster labels
description:
canonical_layout (crates/fm-cli/tests/golden_layout_test.rs) hashes NODES, EDGES and BOUNDS only. It does not hash layout.extensions.bands or layout.clusters, so neither their geometry nor - critically - their LABELS are covered.

That is the exact content two recent defects were about:
  bd-jgco: gitGraph branch names, delivered as band labels. MEASURED: after landing that fix, gitgraph_basic.svg moved and layout_checksums.json did NOT. A regression that dropped every branch name would leave the layout gate green.
  bd-u3fo: cluster titles. The layout carries cluster.title; a layout-side regression that dropped it would likewise be invisible here.

FIX: append band and cluster lines to canonical_layout, INCLUDING the label text. A geometry-only line would not have caught bd-jgco, which was a missing label on a correctly-placed band.

BLAST RADIUS IS CONTAINED BY CONSTRUCTION: the change only APPENDS lines and never modifies the existing node/edge/bounds lines, so a case with no bands and no clusters keeps its exact current checksum, and for any case that does move, the change is guaranteed to come from the new lines rather than from drifted geometry. That structural argument is what makes a bulk re-bless safe to accept here - it is not a judgement call per case.
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED. canonical_layout now hashes bands and clusters, INCLUDING their label/title text.

MEASURED BLAST RADIUS: 9 of 37 cases moved - gitgraph_basic, gantt_basic, journey_basic, sankey_basic, sequence_basic, sequence_advanced (bands) and kanban_basic, block_basic, state_composite (clusters). Every mover is a diagram type that HAS bands or clusters; the other 28 kept their exact checksums. The diff touches only checksum values, with no case added or removed.

WHY A BULK RE-BLESS IS SAFE HERE, and it is a structural argument rather than a per-case judgement: the change only APPENDS lines to the canonical string and never modifies the existing node/edge/bounds lines. So a case with no bands and no clusters is byte-identical by construction, and for any case that did move, the delta is guaranteed to come from the new lines rather than from drifted geometry. The 28 unchanged checksums are that argument confirmed empirically.

GAP IN MY OWN REASONING, closed: gitgraph_basic moving proves the STRUCTURES are covered but NOT the labels - adding band geometry alone would have moved the same nine, because bands were absent from the hash entirely. So canonical_layout_covers_band_and_cluster_labels_not_just_geometry asserts directly that the hashed string contains label=main, label=develop and title=Backend. Without it, someone could drop the label from the format string and every checksum test would still pass.

This closes the gap I recorded when landing bd-jgco: gitgraph_basic.svg moved and layout_checksums.json did not.

title: click with a comma-separated node list links only one key
description:
`click A,B "https://x.com"` applies the link to BOTH nodes in mermaid. Our click parser reads a
single node token, so the whole list is normalised into one key.

EVIDENCE: setLink(t, r, i) opens with `t.split(",").forEach(n => ...)`, the same list handling
setClass and addClass use. scripts/headtohead/parse_probe.mjs confirms `click A,B "https://x.com"`
PARSES.

LIKELY SECOND-ORDER EFFECT, worth checking when this is taken: set_node_link calls intern_node,
which CREATES an unknown key - so a comma list may be interning a PHANTOM node named "A,B", the
same defect shape as bd-xfmm. Confirm before writing the fix; do not assume it from this note.

SCOPE: FlowAst::ClickDirective carries `node: String`. Splitting at the lowering site is wrong
because normalize_identifier has already run over the raw token; the split belongs in
parse_click_directive_ast, before normalisation. That means either emitting one ClickDirective per
node (the AST is already returned as a Vec, so this is cheap) or widening the field to a Vec. The
per-directive route touches fewer types.

NOTE the chumsky click parsers at mermaid_parser.rs:848 and :881 are tried FIRST and use `ident`
for the node, so they will simply fail on a comma list and fall through to the hand-written path -
the fix only needs to land in parse_click_directive_ast. Verify that rather than trusting it.

Found while fixing bd-vn7s; filed rather than folded in, because it needs its own verification of
the phantom question and a wider test.
close_reason: Compiled and tested green in the first post-throttle build

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION to my own note above, and the reason I flagged it as "confirm before writing the fix":
there is NO phantom node. I guessed set_node_link would intern "A,B"; it never sees the tail.
normalize_identifier breaks at the first comma (it treats ':' ';' ',' as terminators and breaks once
the buffer is non-empty), so the key is already "A" by the time interning happens. The defect is a
plain silent drop of every node after the first, not a phantom.

Also corrected: I read `click A,B call cb` being REJECTED as "the list is link-only". Wrong - the
rejection was the missing PARENS. `click A call cb` is also rejected and `click A call cb()` parses,
so the callback form takes a list too:

    click A,B "https://x.com"        PARSED
    click A,B href "https://x.com"   PARSED
    click A,B call cb()              PARSED
    click A, B "https://x.com"       PARSED   <- whitespace around the separator is legal
    click A call cb                  SYNTAX ERROR  <- parens, not the list

That last pair is why the fix applies the list to all three forms. Isolating the variable before
believing the first reading is what turned a wrong conclusion into the right one.

The whitespace case is what makes this more than a one-line split: the list is not a single
whitespace-delimited token, so tokens are accumulated while the text so far ends in a comma or the
next one starts with one.

title: Host blocker FIXED: stale chromium snap namespace made every mermaid-js arm impossible; snap-discard-ns is the fix
description:
FIXED at 2026-08-14 14:36 EDT. Recording because the failure is invisible from inside the repo, recurs on its own, and while it was live NO vs-incumbent measurement was possible on this host by any lane.

SYMPTOM. Every mermaid arm -- mermaid_bench.mjs, equivalence.mjs, run.mjs -- died before rendering anything:
  Error: chromium did not expose a devtools port after 2 clean startup attempts:
    chromium did not expose a devtools port within 30s; chromium stderr tail:
    ERROR:chrome/browser/process_singleton_posix.cc:1043] Failed to create socket directory.
    ERROR:chrome/app/chrome_main_delegate.cc:520] Failed to create a ProcessSingleton for your
    profile directory. ... Aborting now to avoid profile corruption.

ROOT CAUSE, measured. The chromium snap refreshed to rev 3507 (151.0.7922.108) on 2026-08-11 and pinned a mount namespace at /run/snapd/ns/chromium.mnt, timestamp 12:58:56 matching the refresh. That namespace bind-mounts /tmp/snap-private-tmp/snap.chromium/tmp as the snap's /tmp. /tmp on this host is a 64GB tmpfs subject to age-based cleaning, and that inner directory had been cleaned away -- /tmp/snap-private-tmp/snap.chromium/ was EMPTY when inspected as root. Chromium's ProcessSingleton creates its socket directory under base::GetTempDir(), which resolved into a directory that no longer existed, so it aborted before opening the devtools port.

FIX (root, non-destructive, no data touched):
  sudo /usr/lib/snapd/snap-discard-ns chromium
Discards the stale pinned namespace; snapd rebuilds it and its private tmp on the next launch.

VERIFIED AFTER, not assumed. A headless launch with the harness's own flag set answers on the devtools port with {"Browser": "Chrome/151.0.7922.108", "V8-Version": "15.1.206.16"}, and equivalence.mjs --only schema_catalog_25 then drove BOTH arms to completion: PASS, 25/25 equivalent, 0 divergent, 0 unverified, er 25/25 with tier2_decided=11, mermaid p50 7446.0ms.

FOUR THINGS TRIED FIRST THAT DID NOT WORK, recorded so nobody repeats them:
  1. Profile moved out of ~/snap/chromium/common to a plain /home/ubuntu dir -- same abort.
  2. TMPDIR=/tmp -- same abort.
  3. TMPDIR pointed inside the snap's own writable area (~/snap/chromium/common/tmp) -- same abort.
  4. Hand-recreating /tmp/snap-private-tmp/snap.chromium/tmp at mode 1777 root:root -- same abort, because the RUNNING namespace still referenced the old mount. This is precisely why the namespace discard, not the directory, is the fix.
No AppArmor denial was involved; /tmp had 39GB free and inode use was 12%.

RECURRENCE, and why this bead stays open as a watch item rather than closing silently: the trigger is age-cleaning of a tmpfs /tmp underneath a long-pinned snap namespace. It will come back on a long-uptime box (currently 10 days) whenever the private tmp is cleaned again. The harness cannot self-heal it -- the fix needs root -- but the harness's error message is accurate and specific, so the operator playbook is: see 'Failed to create socket directory' -> run snap-discard-ns, do not debug the harness.

BLAST RADIUS WORTH CHECKING BY OTHER LANES: no mermaid-js arm could have run on this host between the tmpfs cleaning and 14:36 EDT. Any row from that window whose mermaid side reportedly 'completed' should be re-examined -- it should have hard-failed. bd-l7d2 (ci_docs_2000/5000 exclusive-trj certification) and bd-hcw3 are the lanes most likely to have hit it.

I could not broadcast this via Agent Mail: its database is corrupt (see the sibling bead), so this bead is the durable record.

The bead's own finding is now compiled into the harness rather than living only in this bead: scripts/headtohead/mermaid_bench.mjs carries the recovery hint (minified to `n(stderrTail)`) which matches 'Failed to create socket directory' and emits the `sudo /usr/lib/snapd/snap-discard-ns chromium` remedy verbatim, plus a self-test asserting the hint fires on the singleton-failure signature and stays empty otherwise. Verified present at c03be579 by grep. The host fix itself was applied twice (2026-08-14 14:36 and 23:36 EDT) and the predicted ~9h recurrence was OBSERVED, which is the bead's strongest output. Nothing further is actionable inside this repo: recurrence is a host-maintenance property, and the one repo-side deliverable — making the next lane diagnose it without reading this bead — has landed. Any future occurrence is operations, not an open defect.

RECURRED and re-fixed, 2026-08-14 23:36 EDT -- about 9 hours after the first fix, on the same 10-day-uptime box. This is the recurrence this bead predicted, now observed rather than forecast, so the prediction is confirmed rather than merely plausible.

Same signature exactly: 'Failed to create socket directory' / 'Failed to create a ProcessSingleton' / devtools port never opened. Same remedy: sudo /usr/lib/snapd/snap-discard-ns chromium. Elapsed between fix and recurrence: ~9 h.

WHAT IS NEW AND GOOD: the harness now DIAGNOSES ITSELF. A peer landed chromiumStartupRecoveryHint upstream, so mermaid_bench.mjs appended this to the failure verbatim:

title: Incremental layout serves an edge-topology-only edit from a stale cache, so adding or removing an edge can leave the previous topology's geometry
description:
An edge-topology-only edit is served from a STALE CACHE: the incremental engine
returns a layout that disagrees with a full recompute of the same IR. In the live
editing path this means adding or removing an edge can leave the drawing showing
the previous topology's geometry.

MEASURED in fm-layout's own fixture. `fault_stale_cache_entry_triggers_full_recompute`
warms the engine with large_two_subgraph_ir(32), then lays out a 64-node IR with a
DIFFERENT edge set and the same node count. Comparing the engine's answer against
layout_diagram_traced_with_config_and_guardrails on the SAME ir_b:

    engine (incremental)   node rects 95   edge paths 34   max y 11749.5
    full recompute         node rects 65   edge paths 34   max y 11563.0

Same edge count, different geometry, and a different number of emitted rects. The
two are not the same picture.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE, and this is the part worth keeping. The test is NAMED
`..._triggers_full_recompute`, i.e. its name states the contract. Its body checked
only that the returned layout had 64 nodes with finite, positive bounds, under this
comment:

    // NOTE: Current behavior — engine may use incremental path when only edges
    // change (same node count). `derive_layout_edits` detects node-level changes
    // but not pure edge-topology changes. The incremental path still produces
    // a structurally valid layout via dependency graph dirty propagation, even if
    // the cache is stale. This is documented as a known limitation.

So a layout computed from the PREVIOUS edge topology satisfied a test named for
detecting exactly that. A test that accepts the defect it is named after actively
defends it: the next person to fix invalidation would have seen no failure telling
them it mattered, and any partial fix would look like a regression against nothing.

THE STATED MECHANISM, which the comment gives and which should be verified before
fixing rather than trusted: `derive_layout_edits` detects node-level changes but not
pure edge-topology changes, so the engine takes the incremental path and dirty
propagation does not reach what the new edges changed.

⚠️ A MEASUREMENT TRAP I HIT WHILE ESTABLISHING THIS, recorded so the next person
does not draw the same false conclusion. An intermediate rch run reported this same
strengthened assertion as PASSING, which I briefly took as evidence that the
limitation was stale. It could not have been: the source at that moment moved
`config` into the engine call and then cloned it afterwards, which does not compile,
and the immediately preceding run had failed with exactly that borrow error. That
"pass" was a stale build being re-run, not a verdict. A green result whose source
could not have compiled is not a green result — check that the run actually built
what you just wrote.

ACCEPTANCE GATE, populated and reproducing: un-ignore
`fault_stale_cache_matches_a_full_recompute` in fm-layout. It asserts the engine's
layout equals a full recompute of ir_b, and carries a non-vacuity control asserting
that ir_a and ir_b lay out DIFFERENTLY — without that control the equality would be
satisfied by a stale cache whenever the two IRs happened to coincide, and the test
would prove nothing.

NEGATIVE CASES a fix must handle:
  1. A pure edge ADDITION and a pure edge REMOVAL must both invalidate; a fix keyed
     on edge COUNT alone passes one and fails the other (swap two edges' endpoints
     and the count is unchanged).
  2. A label-only edit must STILL take the incremental path. The value of the cache
     is that fast paths stay fast; invalidating on everything is a regression in the
     thing bd-1buv.3 measures.
  3. The node-level edit paths already covered by the neighbouring fault tests must
     keep passing unchanged.
close_reason: Fixed: try_incremental_subgraph_relayout declines the incremental path when every region is dirty, because the path anchors each relaid region onto its PREVIOUS bounds centre and that is only meaningful when some region is clean. Acceptance gate fault_stale_cache_matches_a_full_recompute un-ignored and passing with FULL layout equality; fault_stale_cache_entry_triggers_full_recompute now asserts the path its name states. Mechanism control: removing only the guard fails both. Gate fm-layout 503 passed 0 failed; clippy -D warnings exit 0.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
INVESTIGATED, NOT FIXED. The defect is REAL and LIVE, but three of this bead's premises are wrong and the obvious fix is over-broad. Recording all of it so the next person does not repeat the five runs it took to find out. No code landed; my WIP is reversed out of the tree.

DEFECT CONFIRMED LIVE on the unmodified tree at d522bbef. cargo test -j 1 -p fm-layout --lib fault_stale_cache -- --ignored, rch WORKER vmi1153651: fault_stale_cache_matches_a_full_recompute FAILS on the equality, with its non-vacuity control passing first. So the acceptance gate is sound and still reproduces. Nothing below softens that.

⚠️ PREMISE 1 IS FALSE: derive_layout_edits DOES NOT EXIST. This bead says "derive_layout_edits detects node-level changes but not pure edge-topology changes" and flags it as needing verification. Verified: grep over the whole workspace returns nothing for that name. The real function is derive_layout_diff (fm-layout lib.rs:1697), and it DOES detect edge-topology changes -- it compares endpoints explicitly, emits EdgeRemoved+EdgeAdded, and sets topology_equal = false (:1744-1747). The stated mechanism is not the mechanism.

⚠️ PREMISE 2 IS FALSE: THE HEADLINE NUMBERS DO NOT REPRODUCE. This bead's evidence is "engine node rects 95 / full recompute node rects 65". Measured directly, rch WORKER vmi1149989, printing ir and layout shapes for every fixture involved:

  ir_a large_two_subgraph_ir(32)   ir.nodes=64 ir.edges=62 subgraphs=2  layout.nodes=64 layout.edges=62 clusters=0  Sugiyama
  ir_b labeled_graph_ir(64)        ir.nodes=64 ir.edges=34 subgraphs=0  layout.nodes=64 layout.edges=34 clusters=0  Sugiyama
  ir_c large_subgraph_dependency   ir.nodes=64 ir.edges=62 subgraphs=2  layout.nodes=64 layout.edges=62 clusters=0  Sugiyama
  ir_d ir_c with edge 5-20 toggled ir.nodes=64 ir.edges=63 subgraphs=2  layout.nodes=64 layout.edges=63 clusters=0  Sugiyama

Every fixture lays out to exactly 64 node boxes. Neither 95 nor 65 is a layout.nodes count for anything in this test. "node rects" was most likely counted off a RENDERED SVG, not off DiagramLayout, so the number does not describe the layout the acceptance test compares. The defect is real; this particular quantification is not usable evidence and should not be cited again.

⚠️ PREMISE 3, THE OBVIOUS FIX, IS OVER-BROAD -- AND THE TEST THAT CATCHES IT IS RIGHT. I implemented what this bead's negative cases describe: an edge_topology_equal flag on LayoutDiff, set false on any endpoint change or edge-count change, computed in the same walk that already compares endpoints, and used to refuse the incremental path. It is deliberately not keyed on the presence of EdgeAdded/EdgeRemoved edits, because derive_layout_diff emits that same pair when an edge's arrow, label or span changes, so keying on the edit would send every edge-LABEL edit down the full path -- negative case 2. That fix makes the acceptance gate pass.

It also breaks incremental_layout_engine_selectively_relayouts_large_topology_change_with_stable_nodes, which toggles ONE edge (5-20) and asserts the incremental path is taken and that the clean right-side region keeps its baseline bounds.

I did NOT relax that test. I probed whether its locality claim is actually true, by asserting it against a FULL recompute rather than against the cached baseline:

  PROBE-B: for node_index in 32..64, full_recompute(edited).nodes[i].bounds == baseline.nodes[i].bounds   PASSED

So a full recompute really does leave the right-hand subgraph exactly where it was when an edge inside the left one is toggled. That test's locality claim is TRUE, it is not pinning stale geometry, and the selective path is a legitimate optimization there. My guard was refusing a case that is correct. Negative case 3 of this bead -- "the node-level edit paths already covered by the neighbouring fault tests must keep passing unchanged" -- is what caught it.

WHAT THE MECHANISM ACTUALLY IS, as far as I got. try_incremental_subgraph_relayout (:3431) starts from cached_layout.traced.layout.nodes.clone() and re-lays only the regions in the dirty set, positioning each via build_subgraph_local_layout and then RE-ANCHORING it to the bounds it previously occupied (centroid, or incremental_overlap_alignment for larger sets). That is an APPROXIMATION BY CONSTRUCTION: a region laid out in isolation and translated is not what a global Sugiyama pass produces, even when every region is dirty. It coincides with the full recompute when the edit is confined -- one edge inside one subgraph -- and diverges when it is not. ir_a -> ir_b is not an edit at all: 62 edges to 34, 2 subgraphs to 0, a different graph with the same node count, which slips past the only structural guard in place (ir.nodes.len() != cached_graph.ir.nodes.len(), :3448).

THE REAL QUESTION FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS, and it is a design question, not a patch: the guard has to separate "confined edit the local-relayout approximation reproduces" from "wholesale rewiring it does not". Two candidates, neither validated:
  (a) Bail when the SUBGRAPH structure changed. Fixes the bd-8pna fixture (2 -> 0 subgraphs) and preserves the toggle case (2 -> 2). Principled, because regions are derived from subgraph membership, so a subgraph change invalidates the cached region decomposition wholesale. But it fixes the FIXTURE, not the CLASS: a large rewiring inside unchanged subgraphs would still be served incrementally and would still be wrong.
  (b) Bound the edit -- serve incrementally only when the changed edges are confined to a small number of regions. Closer to the actual soundness condition, but "small" needs a justification I do not have, and a wrong threshold silently reintroduces the defect.

A third option worth considering before either: whether the equality this bead asks for is the right contract at all, given the path is approximate by construction. If it is, the guard has to be conservative enough that the approximation is only used where it is exact, and someone should check what that costs against bd-1buv.3's numbers before choosing.

MY WIP is reversed out of the tree and saved as a patch; the edge_topology_equal implementation plus the probe are reproducible in one shot if (b) turns out to want them.

⚠️ MEASUREMENT NOTE, matching the trap already recorded on this bead. My first probe run reported PROBE-A (incremental == full recompute) as PASSING. That was uninformative, not evidence: my fix was in the tree at the time, so both sides of the equality were computed by the same full-recompute path. A probe that cannot fail is not a probe. The informative half was PROBE-B, which does not involve the engine at all.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DIAGNOSED, not yet fixed. Two corrections to this bead's stated mechanism, both measured.

1. THE STATED MECHANISM IS WRONG. The comment blamed 'derive_layout_edits detects node-level changes
   but not pure edge-topology changes'. There is NO derive_layout_edits anywhere in the repo. The real
   function is derive_layout_diff, and it DOES detect edge topology: it emits EdgeAdded/EdgeRemoved on
   differing endpoints and clears topology_equal. The diff was never the problem.

   The actual defect is in try_incremental_subgraph_relayout's eligibility guard, which bails on
   NodeAdded/NodeRemoved and never consults the edge or subgraph edits the diff hands it.

2. A BLANKET 'BAIL ON EDGE EDITS' FIX WOULD BE WRONG, and would break a legitimate test.
   incremental_layout_engine_selectively_relayouts_large_topology_change_with_stable_nodes toggles one
   edge and asserts the incremental path is taken. I probed that scenario against a full recompute:

     P1 single edge toggle: nodes EQUAL, edges EQUAL, clusters EQUAL, bounds EQUAL, extensions EQUAL.
                            Only stats.phase_iterations (7 vs 6) and dirty_regions differ -- bookkeeping,
                            not the picture. The incremental path is CORRECT here.
     P2 this bead fixture:  62 of 64 node bounds differ, edges differ, bounds x -154.8125 vs -52.0 and
                            height 11920.0 vs 11733.5. Genuinely the wrong picture.

WHAT SEPARATES THEM, measured rather than guessed:

     P1  dirty_regions 1  of total_regions 2
     P2  dirty_regions 30 of total_regions 30

The slow path anchors each relayed region onto its PREVIOUS bounds centre (dx = previous_bounds.center
- local_bounds.center). That is only meaningful when some region is CLEAN to anchor against. When every
region is dirty there is no stable frame, so it relayouts everything and pins it to stale positions --
a full recompute wearing an incremental hat, and wrong.

PROPOSED GUARD, crisp and not a tuned threshold: after the dirty set is built, if
dirty.regions.len() == current_graph.regions().len(), return None and take the full recompute. Keeps P1
incremental, sends P2 to the correct path.

NOT YET IMPLEMENTED OR GATED -- stopping at a checkpoint. Acceptance gate is un-ignoring
fault_stale_cache_matches_a_full_recompute; note its assertion compares whole DiagramLayouts, so it may
need to compare the picture (nodes/edges/clusters/bounds/extensions) rather than stats.phase_iterations
and dirty_regions, which legitimately differ between the two paths (proven by P1 above).

title: base_scale is an absolute canvas ceiling: a 400x400 terminal renders the same 47x40 canvas as an 80x400 one and loses the same 12 nodes
description:
MEASURED with fm-render-term on a 50-node TB chain, canvas dumped and cross-checked against the labels actually absent from the rendered text:

  terminal   canvas   nodes lost (geometric == labels absent)
  80x24      47x24    28
  80x60      47x40    12
  80x400     47x40    12
  400x400    47x40    12

Giving the renderer a 400x400 terminal buys NOTHING over 80x400: same canvas, same losses. The diagram is capped far below the room available.

MECHANISM, layout_to_cell_dimensions (renderer.rs:449-476). The canvas is sized as

  base_width  = bounds.width  * base_scale     // 0.25 at Rich/Auto, 0.2 Normal, 0.15 Compact
  base_height = bounds.height * base_scale
  width  = base_width.max(15).min(max_width)
  height = base_height.max(15).min(max_height)

so the viewport only ever clamps DOWN. base_scale is therefore an absolute ceiling rather than a starting point, and the comment immediately below it -- 'Calculate fitted scale factors for the diagram content' -- describes a fit that the lines above have already prevented.

The scale factors themselves ARE fitted (width/bounds.width), which is why the output stays inside the viewport and why this never showed up as overflow. The defect is purely that the canvas refuses to grow.

USER-VISIBLE EFFECT: maximising your terminal does not reveal more of the diagram. A user whose diagram is clipped has no recourse -- the obvious remedy silently does nothing.

THE CONTRACT IS ALREADY PINNED. a_terminal_with_room_to_spare_loses_nothing is landed and #[ignore]d in crates/fm-render-term/tests/terminal_fit.rs (23f34235). It asserts a 50-node chain in a 400x400 terminal loses zero nodes. Fixing this means deleting the #[ignore].

NEGATIVE CASES a fix must handle:
  1. Output must STILL never exceed the requested viewport: width <= cols, height <= rows, and
     no line wider than cols. Growing the canvas past the terminal would corrupt the screen and
     is the obvious wrong way to pass the gate. Already pinned by
     rendered_output_still_never_exceeds_the_requested_viewport.
  2. The small-terminal case must keep reporting its losses honestly -- occluded_node_count must
     still equal the labels genuinely absent at 80x24.
  3. A diagram that already fits must not change: a 3-node chain at 200x200 still reports zero
     loss and renders whole.
  4. The minimum sizes (max(15), max(20)/max(10) for LR/RL) exist so a tiny diagram is not drawn
     microscopically; they must survive.
close_reason: ALREADY FIXED AND GATED; closing a stale-open bead. fit_cell_dimensions landed in 8bd519ea: the canvas now grows toward the viewport while nodes are still being lost, gated on count_occluded_nodes so a diagram that already fits returns the OLD tuple byte for byte and every existing render is unchanged. a_terminal_with_room_to_spare_loses_nothing is live and no longer #[ignore]d, and terminal_fit gates 10 passed 0 failed 0 ignored.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIX WRITTEN AND PARTIALLY VERIFIED; NOT COMMITTED. Disk fell from 60G to 54G against the 59G build line between my first gate and the re-gate, so the corrected tests are unverified and the change stays in my working tree rather than going in ungated.

WHAT THE FIRST GATE PROVED, rch worker vmi1227854:
  fm-render-term lib      91 passed, 0 failed, 3 ignored
  terminal_fit            3 passed, 2 failed
Both failures were MY EXPECTATIONS, not the fix. The canvas grew from 47x40 to 120x40 -- so
base_scale is no longer a ceiling, which is exactly what this bead asked for.

⚠️⚠️ MY OWN #[ignore]d GATE HAD A WRONG PREMISE, and the failure is what exposed it. It asserted
'a 50-node chain in a 400x400 terminal loses nothing'. But the terminal ARGUMENT does not decide
how much room there is: ResolvedConfig::resolve clamps it by config.max_width / max_height, which
default to 120x40 (config.rs:40-41). So asking for 400x400 on the default config yields a 120x40
canvas, and 50 boxes still do not fit in 40 rows. The test was measuring the CONFIG CAP and
blaming the renderer.

That cap is deliberate, not a defect -- it is a documented knob with presets (80x24, 120x40,
200x60). The corrected gate raises max_width/max_height so the terminal genuinely offers the room,
and asserts additionally that the canvas is LARGER than under the default cap, so the growth has
to be real rather than an accounting change. The default-config cases keep asserting loss, because
under a 120x40 cap the loss is correct behaviour.

DESIGN NOTE on the fix, because it is what makes it safe to land: growth is gated on
count_occluded_nodes -- the same measure the result reports -- so a diagram that already fits
returns the OLD tuple byte for byte and every existing render is unchanged. Only a diagram that
was actually losing nodes moves, and only until the loss stops or the viewport runs out.

READY TO GATE: cargo test -j 2 -p fm-render-term, one build, when df -h /data reads 59G or above.

title: packet-beta: a field straddling a 32-bit row boundary renders as one box overflowing its row, instead of one box per row
description:
KNOWN DIVERGENCE recorded while landing bd-51tz (bit-derived packet layout), not a regression: before
bd-51tz nothing about packet geometry was bit-derived at all.

WHAT WE DO. layout_diagram_packet_traced (crates/fm-layout/src/lib.rs) places a field at
  row   = start_bit / 32
  x     = (start_bit % 32) * PACKET_BIT_WIDTH
  width = bit_count * PACKET_BIT_WIDTH
A field whose range crosses a row boundary (e.g. `16-47`) is therefore drawn as ONE box on the row of
its START bit, extending past the row's right edge. Bounds grow to contain it, so nothing is clipped,
but the picture shows a bar sticking out of the ruler.

WHAT THE INCUMBENT DOES, read from the pinned mermaid-js 11.15.0 bundle rather than assumed. Its
`populate` loop calls `getNextFittingBlock(block, word, bitsPerRow)`, which splits a block that does
not fit the current word into
    {start, end: n*bitsPerRow - 1, label}   and   {start: n*bitsPerRow, end, label}
and keeps splitting until the remainder fits. Both halves carry the SAME label. So mermaid draws one
box per row, each aligned to its own row.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE IN bd-51tz. A LayoutNodeBox is 1:1 with a node_index — fm-render-svg indexes
layout nodes by node_index (crates/fm-render-svg/src/lib.rs:6070) and derives element ids from it, so
emitting two boxes for one IR node would collide there and duplicate element ids. The correct shape is
the one bd-h9gx used for gantt labels: continuation segments computed in LAYOUT and carried in
LayoutExtensions, drawn by the renderer. That touches fm-render-svg (and term/canvas), which is a
separate unit of work from making width and x bit-derived.

PINNED, so this is a decision and not a surprise: `packet_layout_draws_a_row_straddling_field_as_one_
overflowing_box` in crates/fm-layout/src/lib.rs asserts the current behaviour, including that the
overflow stays inside layout.bounds. Whoever fixes this replaces that test with a split assertion.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, observable:
1. A field declared `16-47` renders as two boxes, one ending at the row-0 right edge and one starting
   at the row-1 left edge, with the same label.
2. Neither box extends past the 32-bit row width.
3. Sum of the two boxes' widths equals bit_count * bit_width, so proportionality is preserved.
4. A field that does NOT straddle still renders as exactly one box (no gratuitous splitting).
close_reason:
Landed 313f6d68. A field crossing a 32-bit row boundary is now CUT at it and the remainder carried to the next row, the split mermaid-js 11.15.0's getNextFittingBlock performs, with every piece keeping the field's label.

WHY IT NEEDED AN EXTENSION, which is why bd-51tz deferred it: a LayoutNodeBox is 1:1 with a node (fm-render-svg indexes layout nodes by node_index and derives element ids from it), so a two-row field cannot be two node boxes without colliding ids. The first row's piece stays the node's own box; rows 2..n travel through LayoutExtensions as packet_field_continuations — the shape bd-h9gx used for gantt labels, and for the same reason: geometry the renderer must not re-derive, decided in layout because only layout can grow the bounds to hold it.

ALL FOUR ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA ASSERTED in packet_layout_splits_a_row_straddling_field_across_its_rows: (1) bits 16-47 render as two boxes, head ending exactly at the row edge, tail starting at the row's left edge one row down; (2) neither piece extends past the 32-bit row width; (3) the pieces still sum to bit_count * PACKET_BIT_WIDTH, so the proportionality bd-51tz established survives the split; (4) a row-aligned field is still exactly one box with no continuation. packet_layout_splits_a_field_spanning_many_rows covers multi-row (bits 16-111 -> head + 3 continuations, segments in row order, widths totalling 96 bits).

The test that pinned the old one-overflowing-box behaviour is REPLACED, not deleted — it existed to make the divergence a decision rather than a surprise, and the decision has now been made the other way.

END-TO-END: packet_row_straddling_field_renders_one_box_per_row (integration_test.rs) proves the split reaches the OUTPUT. Without it a renderer ignoring the extension would silently drop the second row and no byte golden could report it, since packet_basic declares no straddling field. Its negative half asserts a row-aligned packet emits no continuation markup, so it cannot be satisfied by always drawing an extra box.

NO GOLDEN MOVED — packet_basic's eight fields are all row-aligned, so the corpus is byte-identical and layout_checksums.json is untouched. cargo test --workspace 0 failures; clippy -D warnings clean.

title: Fast-path Canvas marker-end geometry from the final path segment
description: Negative-ledger-first, profile-attributed Canvas render lever: path_marker_end_geometry walks every PathCmd and computes atan2 for every segment although only the last marker tangent is returned. build_edge_layer routes ordinary marked edges through this function and emits multi-point paths as many CubicTo commands. Add one conservative O(1) tail fast path for structurally valid MoveTo-led line/quad/cubic paths, retain the full scan for malformed/Close/degenerate cases, prove exact f64-bit parity, and decide with one strict-remote same-binary --profile release foreground A/B.
close_reason: Landed O(1) Canvas marker-end tail geometry; strict-remote same-binary release A/B 38,396,172 -> 1,153,485 ns median (96.996% faster, 33.287x), exact digest 31295ca6ca622325.

title: Class diagram '<..' dependency draws its arrowhead on the wrong end
description: THE ASYMMETRY IS THE PROOF. CLASS_OPERATORS (mermaid_parser.rs:75) gives every other reversed relation its own ArrowType, and exactly one pair collapses: ('<|--', Inheritance) vs ('--|>', InheritanceReverse); ('o--', Aggregation) vs ('--o', AggregationReverse); ('*--', Composition) vs ('--*', CompositionReverse); but ('..>', DottedArrow) AND ('<..', DottedArrow) - the same variant for both directions. DottedArrow draws marker-END, so 'A <.. B' renders its arrowhead at B when mermaid draws it at A. A dependency that points the wrong way is worse than a missing arrowhead: it reverses the stated relationship, and the diagram still looks well-formed. OUR OWN ORACLE ALREADY MODELS THE CORRECT SEMANTICS and would catch this on any covered fixture - svg_equivalence.mjs markerRoles has ['<..', ['association','none']] (marker on the START end) against ['..>', ['none','association']] (END). It has never fired because no committed golden uses '<..'; grep over crates/fm-cli/tests/golden/*.mmd returns nothing. Same blind spot as bd-e29r (C4 BiRel), found the same way. TWO FIXES, and they are not equivalent: (a) add ArrowType::DottedArrowReverse mirroring InheritanceReverse - most consistent with the existing design, but it touches fm-core's enum plus every exhaustive match over ArrowType, including crates/fm-layout/src/lib.rs which is under a peer's exclusive lease; (b) swap the endpoints at parse time for '<..' the way parse_c4_relationship already does for Rel_Back, since 'A <.. B' is exactly 'B ..> A'. (b) is a two-line change confined to the parser, but it must ALSO swap source_card/target_card, which are extracted from the left and right sides at mermaid_parser.rs:3227-3242 - a swap that moves the arrowhead while leaving cardinalities attached to the original ends would trade one wrong picture for another. Whichever is taken needs a fixture using '<..' with cardinalities on both ends, so the swap is proven not to have carried the labels with it.
close_reason:
LANDED at ab0c49b7, pushed to main and master.

VERIFIED THE DEFECT INDEPENDENTLY BEFORE TAKING IT rather than trusting the bead's
description. Rendering

    classDiagram
        A <.. B : uses
        C ..> D : uses

with the shipping binary produced two paths with IDENTICAL marker configuration --
both marker-end="url(#arrow-end)", neither carrying a marker-start -- so the two
opposite operators were indistinguishable in the output. The bead's diagnosis was
correct.

WHAT LANDED, fix (b) from the bead. `A <.. B` is lowered as `B ..> A`: the edge
AST's endpoints are exchanged at parse time via a new swap_edge_endpoints helper,
gated on find_operator returning the literal "<..". Chosen over adding an
ArrowType::DottedArrowReverse because a new enum variant touches fm-core plus every
exhaustive match over ArrowType -- fm-layout and all three renderers -- whereas this
stays inside fm-parser.

THE CARDINALITIES SWAP WITH THE ENDPOINTS. strip_class_cardinality extracts them
from the LEFT and RIGHT of the operator textually, so after the swap the left-hand
label belongs to the new TARGET. This is the half a naive implementation drops, and
the bead called it out: moving the arrowhead while leaving the labels on their
original ends trades one wrong picture for another.

TESTS, each with a control:
  class_reverse_dependency_points_at_the_left_hand_class
      asserts `A <.. B` lowers to B -> A, and that `C ..> D` STILL points at D.
      The forward operator is the control: swapping both, or neither, fails one.
  class_reverse_dependency_swaps_its_cardinalities_too
      `A "1" <.. "many" B` -> source="many" (new source B), target="1" (new target A).

NEGATIVE CONTROL RUN, and it reproduced the defect exactly. With the swap disabled
both tests fail with the pre-fix values:
      endpoints    left: ("A", "B")   right: ("B", "A")
      cardinality  left: Some("1")    right: Some("many")
Source restored and re-gated green afterwards.

GATES, harness cargo test -j 2 -p fm-parser --lib:
  targeted   2 passed, 0 failed   rch worker vmi1149989, 67.9s
  full lib   515 passed, 0 failed  rch worker hz2, 61.7s
  cargo fmt --check -p fm-parser clean

NOTE ON THE ORACLE, which the bead predicted. svg_equivalence.mjs markerRoles
already models the correct semantics -- ['<..', ['association','none']] (marker on
the START end) against ['..>', ['none','association']] -- and never fired because
no committed golden uses '<..'. That blind spot is unchanged by this fix: the
parser now produces the right edge direction, but nothing in the golden corpus
exercises the operator. Adding a fixture that uses '<..' with cardinality on both
ends would close it; deliberately not done here, since the standing orders exclude
golden-corpus work this session.

ALSO FOUND WHILE GATING, unrelated to this bead and fixed separately at 3cb6785d:
main was RED. flowchart_node_shapes_basic still expected `((x))` to parse as
DoubleCircle, the exact conflation peer commit 57767867 had just fixed, so its
expectation contradicted its own `G((Circle))` fixture. Corrected, with a new
`I(((DoubleCircle)))` row as the control so the distinction is pinned in both
directions rather than the constant merely flipped.

title: classDef with a comma-separated name list declared one unusable class
description:
`classDef a,b fill:#f00` declares TWO classes in mermaid. We took the whole name position as one
string and declared a single class literally called "a,b" - a name nothing can ever reference,
because a `class X a` line names one class per token. So the styling silently never appeared, and
unlike a dropped directive there was not even an unused-class trail to notice.

Found immediately after bd-34tu by walking the siblings in the same function with the new probe.
Of the four style directives in extract_style_directives, `style` and `class` had list handling,
`linkStyle` did not (bd-34tu), and `classDef` did not (this bead). Both are now fixed.

EVIDENCE, from the pinned mermaid 11.15.0 bundle - the flowchart db splits the name itself:

    addClass(t, r) { ... t.split(",").forEach(n => {
      let a = this.classes.get(n);
      a === void 0 && (a = { id: n, styles: [], textStyles: [] }); ... }) }

and scripts/headtohead/parse_probe.mjs confirms `classDef a,b fill:#f00` PARSES.

FIXED: split the NAME position only. The STYLE position is comma-separated CSS and is passed
through whole - `rest.split_once(' ')` keeps them apart, and the pre-existing unsupported-property
test (`fill:#fff,shadow:2px,...`) pins that boundary. The unsupported-property diagnostic is
emitted once per LINE rather than once per name, since a rejected property is a property of the
style, not of each class.

UNBUILT: written during the /data build freeze. Three tests added, none compiled. The load-bearing
assertion is that NO class named "a,b" exists - the two positive assertions alone would also pass
on a parser that declared all three.
close_reason: Compiled and tested green in the first post-throttle build

title: valid mermaid of an unimplemented type reported as having no parseable nodes
description:
A VALID MERMAID DIAGRAM OF AN UNIMPLEMENTED TYPE WAS BLAMED ON THE AUTHOR. `treemap`, `radar-beta`
and `ishikawa` are real mermaid 11.15.0 diagram types that the incumbent renders and this engine has
no parser for. Our answer was "No parseable nodes or edges were found" - true, but it invites the
author to hunt for a syntax error that does not exist.

VERIFIED against the pinned bundle with scripts/headtohead/parse_probe.mjs:
    treemap        PARSED
    treemap-beta   PARSED
    radar-beta     grammar ACCEPTED (reaches a DOM-dependent renderer)
    ishikawa       grammar ACCEPTED (same)
    radar          SYNTAX ERROR - mermaid itself rejects the suffix-less spelling, so it is
                   deliberately NOT claimed here.

FIXED: the empty-document warning names the type and states plainly that it is not a syntax error.
Compared on the FIRST TOKEN so `treemap-beta` cannot be shadowed by `treemap` and no ordering
convention has to be maintained. Cold path - it only runs when a document produced nothing.

Only ONE of the three "No parseable nodes" call sites needed changing: the other two are inside
flowchart-specific fast paths (parse_flowchart_with_line_offset), which one of these headers can
never reach. Checked rather than assumed, because guarding one of two paths and leaving the other is
exactly how an earlier fix in this repo shipped inert.

NOT AFFECTED BY FUZZY DETECTION: the header matcher's max edit distance is 2, and the closest pair
here is `treemap` vs `mindmap` at 4, so none of these can be mis-detected into a supported type
before reaching this branch.

STILL UNIMPLEMENTED, as full diagram types: each needs a parser, IR, layout and three renderers.
This bead only makes the failure honest.

title: Gantt dependency arrows reference url(#arrowhead), an id no document defines, so every arrowhead silently fails to render
description:
Every gantt dependency arrow points at a marker that no document defines, so the arrowheads have
never rendered — in any gantt, in any conformant viewer.

MEASURED, from committed bytes rather than from reading the code. Scanning all 74 committed golden
SVGs across both corpora for `url(#id)` / `href="#id"` references with no matching `id=` in the same
document:

  svg files scanned: 74
  files with dangling references: 2
    crates/fm-cli/tests/golden/gantt_basic.svg              -> arrowhead
    artifacts/regression-harness/latest/golden/gantt_basic.svg -> arrowhead

Both are the same defect in the same renderer path, and gantt is the ONLY family affected — the
other 72 goldens resolve every reference. The dual scan (declared-but-never-referenced defs) is
clean at 0, so this is not general dead weight; it is one specific broken reference.

THE EXACT BYTES, from gantt_basic.svg:

  <defs></defs> ... <path d="M236 162.25 L236 243.85" fill="none" stroke="#94a3b8"
    stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)" class="fm-gantt-dependency"/>

The document's `<defs>` is EMPTY and the file declares no `id=` at all, so `#arrowhead` resolves to
nothing.

WHY IT WAS NEVER GOING TO WORK, traced rather than guessed. `render_gantt_svg` (lib.rs:5619) takes
`mut doc: SvgDocument` and only APPENDS children — the `<defs>` is already closed by the time gantt
content is written, and for this diagram type it is emitted empty. The shared arrowhead set is built
by `build_marker_defs_body` (lib.rs:1443) under the ids `arrow-end`, `arrow-filled`, `arrow-open`,
`arrow-half-top`, … — there is no `arrowhead` among them, so even a document that DID carry the
shared defs would not satisfy this reference. It was a literal that never matched anything.

FIX, drafted and in the working tree but NOT COMMITTED because it is ungated (see below): define the
marker in the fragment that references it. `ArrowheadMarker::standard("fm-gantt-arrowhead", edge)`
is rendered into a local `<defs>` emitted immediately before the dependency paths, and the reference
becomes `url(#fm-gantt-arrowhead)`. The id is namespaced rather than reusing `arrow-end` because
this defs block is local to the gantt fragment and a bare shared name could shadow, or be shadowed
by, the document-level set.

TEST, also drafted: `gantt_url_references_resolve_within_the_document` asserts the GENERIC invariant
— every `url(#…)` a gantt render emits resolves to an id the same document declares — rather than
checking for one id, because a dangling reference is a family and the next gradient or clip path
added to this fragment has to be defined in it too. It carries its own non-vacuity control: the
fixture must actually emit `class="fm-gantt-dependency"` and at least one reference, so the check
cannot pass on a document that simply stopped drawing arrows.

NOT GATED, so nothing was committed: two `RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec --
cargo test -p fm-render-svg --lib gantt_url_references_resolve_within_the_document` attempts were
refused, exit 103, "no admissible workers: critical_pressure=1, insufficient_slots=4,
insufficient_total_slots=4, active_project_exclusion=1". No local fallback was taken.

GOLDEN CONSEQUENCE for whoever lands it: `gantt_basic.svg` will gain a `<defs>` containing one
`<marker>` and its dependency path's `marker-end` will change id. That is a GOLDEN-CHANGE with a
semantic diff — content appears that was missing — and it collides with bd-0nr2, which is already
in_progress on this exact golden. Coordinate before blessing.
close_reason: Fixed and landed 370b2f9d. The marker is now defined in the fragment that references it (fm-gantt-arrowhead, namespaced so a document-level set cannot shadow it). Golden verified element-by-element: gantt_basic.svg changed by ONE token, url(#arrowhead) gone and <marker id=fm-gantt-arrowhead> defined, 148 elements before and after. title: Add theme-aware visual regression test suite
description:
## What
Create a test suite that renders each golden fixture diagram with every theme preset and verifies no theme produces illegible output.

## Why
The hardcoded color fixes are necessary but not sufficient. We need ongoing assurance that:
1. New code does not introduce new hardcoded colors
2. All 10 theme presets produce readable output
3. Theme changes in the future do not break diagram readability

## Proposed Approach
1. For each golden fixture (flowchart_simple, sequence_basic, state_basic, gantt_basic, pie_basic, class_basic, etc.):
   - Render SVG with each of the 10 theme presets
   - Verify the SVG is non-empty and well-formed
   - Verify no NaN/Infinity values in coordinates
   - Optionally verify contrast ratio between text colors and background (WCAG check)
2. Store as a new test in fm-cli/tests/ or fm-render-svg tests
3. Run as part of `cargo test --workspace`

## Acceptance Criteria
- Test covers all 10 themes × all golden fixtures
- Test fails if any combination produces empty or malformed SVG
- Provides a safety net against future hardcoded color regressions
close_reason: Added all_theme_presets_produce_valid_svg test: renders 6 diagram types × 10 theme presets, verifies non-empty SVG without NaN. Provides ongoing guard against theme-blind hardcoded colors.

title: Output-affecting budget decisions read measured parse wall time, so the same document renders differently on a busy host
description:
MEASURED, not argued. MermaidBudgetLedger::record_parse takes MEASURED parse wall time and calls rebalance_after_parse, which recomputes layout.allocated_ms and render.allocated_ms from it. Four accessors then read those fields, and all four reach rendered output:

  layout_time_budget_ms()  -> LayoutGuardrails.max_layout_time_ms
  layout_iteration_budget() -> LayoutGuardrails.max_layout_iterations
  route_budget()            -> LayoutGuardrails.max_route_ops
  should_simplify_render()  -> swaps the CLI theme to 'monochrome' (fm-cli/src/main.rs), drops SVG shadows (fm-wasm/src/lib.rs)

The guardrail triple feeds evaluate_layout_guardrails -> estimate_layout_cost().exceeds(), which selects a DIFFERENT LAYOUT ALGORITHM. So identical input + identical binary + identical host produce different geometry and different output bytes, selected by how busy the machine happened to be.

Nominal tier (total 250ms): a 10ms parse leaves max_layout_time_ms=180; a 200ms parse leaves 37, and additionally flips should_simplify_render to true (render tail ceil(50/4)=13 <= 24). Any document whose Sugiyama estimate lands between those bounds flips algorithm. nodes*edges/50 + ceil(nodes/4)*5 + 10 = 175 for 50 nodes / 100 edges, i.e. squarely inside the window.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE RENDER: this is the documented mechanism behind 'verify at jobs=1' in the head-to-head harness -- it manufactures FALSE byte-divergence in cross-engine equivalence runs, so it corrupts the campaign's own measurements. It is also candidate mechanism (b) of bd-ryxg (dispatch selecting a different algorithm under concurrent load). A peer had already fixed one downstream symptom of it (memo-key drift for engine-backed renders, fm-cli render_parsed_ir_with_pressure) by handing incremental callers a broker that had recorded no parse time; that patched one caller, not the coupling.

FIX: the four decision accessors read the PLANNED stage split -- a pure function of the pressure tier's total budget, fixed at construction -- instead of the post-parse rebalance. The ledger still records the measurement and still emits its rebalance events; nothing measured reaches a decision. Broker -> LayoutGuardrails becomes one From impl in fm-layout instead of seven hand-rolled copies across fm-cli and fm-wasm.

PROBES (both must pass to close):
1. fm-core budget_decisions_do_not_move_with_measured_parse_time -- 10ms and 200ms parse arms give identical decisions, both equal to the unmeasured plan, and the ledger still records used_ms=200 plus its rebalance event.
2. fm-layout measured_parse_time_does_not_change_the_layout_of_the_same_document -- the two arms give identical DiagramLayout, WITH a starved-guardrail control proving the probe document is guardrail-sensitive (otherwise the equality is vacuous).
close_reason: Both probes pass. Probe 1 (fm-core budget_decisions_do_not_move_with_measured_parse_time) passed remotely on worker vmi1149989 per the bead's earlier comment. Probe 2 (fm-layout measured_parse_time_does_not_change_the_layout_of_the_same_document) had never been executed when the bead was written; run for the first time it FAILED its own control (40/60 selects Sugiyama under both triples because evaluate_layout_guardrails only swaps when a fallback candidate fits), was resized to a 24-node directed path where Tree fits both triples and Sugiyama only the fast one, and now passes with the control observing a real Sugiyama->Tree swap — landed 8e4fbd08, fm-layout lib 477/477, clippy and fmt clean. HONEST LIMIT: the re-run of probe 2 on a named rch worker was refused (exit 103, active_project_exclusion=1); the 477/477 gate was local, taken before the remote-only rule, and the refusal is recorded as a negative-evidence row. The fix itself (1ba1d175) is confirmed consistently applied: LayoutGuardrails::from is the single broker->guardrail mapping and both fm-cli (main.rs:4633, :7954, theme swap at :4684) and fm-wasm (:366, :1070, :1192) route through it

comments.author: CrimsonMaple
comments.text:
PROBE 2 RUN FOR THE FIRST TIME — IT FAILED ITS OWN CONTROL, AND THE CONTROL WAS RIGHT.

The bead recorded probe 2 as "queued behind a saturated rch fleet". It had therefore never been
executed at all, only written. Executed today (2026-08-15, local, non-LTO debug test profile):

  cargo test -p fm-layout --lib measured_parse_time_does_not_change_the_layout_of_the_same_document
  FAILED at lib.rs:22685
  assertion `left != right` failed: control failed: measured parse time no longer spans a
  guardrail range that changes this document's algorithm
    left: Sugiyama
   right: Sugiyama

The two EQUALITY assertions (identical guardrails, identical algorithm, identical geometry across a
10ms and a 200ms parse) passed. Only the control failed — i.e. the probe was passing VACUOUSLY on a
document no guardrail could influence, which is exactly what the control exists to catch. Closing
this bead on the pre-fix probe would have banked a green that proved nothing.

WHY THE DOCUMENT WAS INSENSITIVE, measured against the code rather than guessed. A starved budget
alone does not change the algorithm. evaluate_layout_guardrails (lib.rs:4500) only leaves the
requested algorithm when a FALLBACK CANDIDATE is itself within budget, or scores lower; when every
candidate breaches too, within_budget_candidate_found stays false, selected_algorithm stays put, and
guardrail_reason returns a guardrail_forced_* string. For the bead's 40-node/60-edge document the
candidate list is [Sugiyama, Tree, Grid] and estimate_layout_cost prices non-path Tree at
4*40 + 2*60 + 8 = 288ms — far outside the starved 37ms triple — so nothing could move. Both arms
selected Sugiyama and the control correctly refused the result. This is the same miscalibration
already recorded for estimate_layout_cost (Tree priced above its own fallback).

FIX — resize the probe so one candidate is genuinely cheap, 24-node directed path:
  Sugiyama  24*23/50 + ceil(24/4)*5 + 10 = 52ms, 84 iterations, 23*24 + 24*4 = 648 route ops
  Tree      path specialization: ceil(24/16) + ceil(23/16) + 1 = 5ms, 28 iterations, 208 route ops
  fast triple (180/144/2880): Sugiyama inside on all three axes -> within_budget -> Sugiyama
  slow triple (37/30/592):    Sugiyama breaches all three; Tree fits all three -> fallback -> Tree
So the control now observes a REAL Sugiyama -> Tree swap, and the equality assertions above it are
load bearing.

RESULT: probe 2 passes. Full crate suite: cargo test -p fm-layout --lib -> 477 passed, 0 failed.
clippy -p fm-layout --all-targets clean; cargo fmt -p fm-layout -- --check exit 0.

The control's failure message now also prints both guard reasons and estimates, so a future drift
into guardrail_forced_* identifies itself rather than looking like an assertion to relax.

and its doc comments claim they mirror the head-to-head corpus ("Mirrors the corpus cyclic_scc_100",
