title: Labelled edges are keyboard-focusable graphics-symbols with NO accessible name: fm-edge-labeled emits no title while its plain fm-edge sibling does
description:
MEASURED over 22 diagram types rendered with the shipping binary, counting role=graphics-symbol groups that carry NO <title> and NO aria-label:

  class                    named   unnamed
  fm-edge (plain)             15         2
  fm-edge-labeled              0        12
  fm-node (all variants)      41         0

Every NODE is named. Every LABELLED EDGE is anonymous.

DIRECT READ from the flowchart 'A[Start] --> B{Choice}; B -->|yes| C; B -->|no| D':
  fm-edge-0  role=graphics-symbol tabindex=0  <title>Start points to Choice</title>
  fm-edge-1  role=graphics-symbol tabindex=0  <title>NONE</title>  aria-label NONE
  fm-edge-2  role=graphics-symbol tabindex=0  <title>NONE</title>  aria-label NONE

fm-edge-0 is the UNLABELLED edge and it is named. fm-edge-1 and fm-edge-2 are the ones the user
labelled 'yes' and 'no', and they announce nothing.

THE INVERSION IS THE POINT: the edges carrying MORE user-authored information are the ones with
LESS accessibility. A user who takes the trouble to label a branch makes that branch invisible to
assistive technology.

WORSE, THEY ARE FOCUSABLE. tabindex=0 puts every one of these in the keyboard tab order, so a
keyboard user tabs onto an element that a screen reader announces as an unnamed graphic. An
unnamed focusable control is a WCAG 4.1.2 Name/Role/Value failure; unnamed-but-unfocusable would
be far less serious.

ASYMMETRIC SIBLING, the pattern already banked from write_escaped_text and the lean-edge work:
two code paths for the same concept, one correct, one not, and the fix is to port the correct
sibling's behaviour rather than invent anything. fm-edge already knows how to build 'X points to
Y'; fm-edge-labeled needs the same, ideally enriched with the label ('Start points to Choice via
yes').

AFFECTED: 10 of 22 diagram types produce at least one unnamed edge -- flowchart, class, er,
sequence, sequence_frag, state, timeline, gitgraph, sankey, c4.

ALSO MEASURED AND CLEAN, so this is a gap not a regression: ZERO of 77 graphics roles carry raw
syntax in an accessible name. The bd-0di8 family (aria-label='accTitle: My Title' on a
graphics-symbol) stays fixed.

NEGATIVE CASES a fix must handle:
  1. The plain fm-edge title must not change -- it is the control and is already correct.
  2. The 2 unnamed plain fm-edge cases must be explained rather than papered over; a name derived
     from endpoints needs endpoints that HAVE names.
  3. Every node must stay named (41/41 today).
  4. The name must be MEANING not SOURCE -- no arrow operators, no ':::', no raw directive text.
     bd-0di8 is the precedent for getting this wrong in the opposite direction.
  5. A diagram with no edges must be unaffected.

BUILD BUDGET: not fixed this turn. df -h /data read 60G against the standing 60G floor all turn,
so no build could start and a renderer change cannot be gated. Evidence and contract recorded so
the fix is short when disk allows.
close_reason:
INVALID - RETRACTED. This bead is my probe's artifact, not a defect. fm-edge-labeled is NOT missing accessible names.

GROUND TRUTH, extracting each full <g> by matching </g> with nesting instead of searching a fixed window:
  fm-edge-0   class=fm-edge          len=210  <title>Start points to Choice
  fm-edge-1   class=fm-edge-labeled  len=569  <title>Choice points to Store with label: yes
  fm-edge-2   class=fm-edge-labeled  len=559  <title>Choice points to End with label: no

Labelled edges are named BETTER than plain ones -- the title carries the label. Corrected totals across all 22 diagram types: 77 of 77 graphics roles named, 0 unnamed. The '19 unnamed' and the whole fm-edge-labeled 0-named/12-unnamed split were false.

THE BUG: the audit searched a FIXED 300-400 character window past each <g ...> for a <title>. A labelled-edge group is 559-569 characters and emits its <title> LAST, after <path>, <rect> and <text>. The title was outside the window. A plain edge group is 210 characters, so its title fit.

⚠️⚠️ WHY THIS ONE FOOLED ME WHERE FIVE EARLIER INSTRUMENT FAILURES DID NOT. The artifact did not look like noise, it looked like a MECHANISM: every long group unnamed, every short group named, split exactly along a real code-path boundary (fm-edge vs fm-edge-labeled). That is the asymmetric-sibling pattern, which genuinely recurs in this repo -- so the false result arrived pre-equipped with an explanation I already believed. A truncation artifact correlated with element SIZE will always align with whatever code path produces bigger elements. I even wrote a non-vacuity control for this audit and it PASSED, because the control's violator was small enough to fit the window: the control tested the wrong dimension.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: reading the source I was about to change. write_labeled_edge_fragment_into's doc comment states that A11Y=true emits role/tabindex AND the trailing <title>. The source contradicted my measurement and the source was right. I had already sent this to BlackThrush as fix-ready work; retracted by message.

CORRECTED AUDIT: scratchpad a11y_fixed.py extracts the full element by construction and carries a control whose <title> sits deliberately 600 characters from the tag, plus a genuinely unnamed element that must still be reported. Both pass. The 0-of-77 raw-syntax result from the original sweep is unaffected -- it read attributes on the opening tag, not the body.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
READ THE INCUMBENT, and it changes the framing of this bead. mermaid-js 11.15.0 rendered through the pinned harness (chromium 151, flowchart_small_10) emits for the WHOLE document:

  aria-roledescription="flowchart-v2"   1 occurrence, on the root
  role="..."                            1 occurrence total
  tabindex                               0 occurrences
  <title>                                0 occurrences

So mermaid gives its edges NO per-element accessibility at all: no role, no name, and it does not put them in the keyboard tab order.

THIS IS NOT A CASE OF US BEING BEHIND THE INCUMBENT. On nodes and plain edges we are well ahead: 41 of 41 nodes and 15 of 17 plain edges carry a <title>, and they are focusable. There is therefore NO incumbent behaviour to copy here, and copying mermaid would mean deleting a feature that is better than theirs. The model for the fix is our OWN fm-edge sibling, not mermaid.

BUT IT ALSO MAKES THIS DEFECT WORSE, NOT MILDER. mermaid never puts an edge in the tab order, so its labelled edges are simply not reachable by keyboard. We DO put them there -- tabindex=0, role=graphics-symbol -- and then give them nothing to announce. An unnamed focusable element is worse than an unfocusable one: the user is made to stop on something that cannot identify itself. So for labelled edges specifically, our output is worse than the incumbent's despite carrying strictly more accessibility markup, which is the sharpest form this kind of bug takes.

Two coherent fixes, and the choice should be deliberate rather than incidental:
  A. Name them, following fm-edge's existing phrase and enriching with the label
     ('Start points to Choice via yes'). Keeps the feature and makes it correct.
  B. Stop making them focusable, matching mermaid. Strictly worse than A, and it would
     silently remove a capability, but it is at least self-consistent.
A is right. The bead's negative cases already pin that the plain-edge title must not change and that the name must be meaning rather than source.

title: Static and abstract class member classifiers are dropped whenever a return type follows the marker
description:
MEASURED at the IR level. IrClassMember.is_static and is_abstract exist and were never set for mermaid's documented method spelling.

  class C {
      +count()$ int
      +draw()* void
  }

  BEFORE  count() static=false abstract=false  |  draw() static=false abstract=false
  AFTER   count() static=TRUE  abstract=false  |  draw() static=false abstract=TRUE

mermaid UNDERLINES static members and ITALICISES abstract ones, so the classifier is the entire visible difference between the two renderings.

MECHANISM: the check was rest.ends_with('$'). The classifier sits against the member's NAME -- for a method, its closing paren -- and a return type may follow it. Testing the end of the whole line therefore only ever fired for a member with NO return type. Two documented placements exist:

  +getName()$ String   marker against the paren, return type after   WAS DROPPED
  int id$              marker at the very end of the line            already worked

FIX: accept both placements and remove ONLY the marker byte, so the return type survives.

⚠️⚠️ I NEARLY SHIPPED AN INVENTED EXPECTATION, and this is the shape-expectation trap turned on its author. My first fix keyed the marker off the end of the member's first TOKEN, which handles '+total$ int'. That form is my invention: mermaid writes attributes type-first, 'int id$', with the marker at the end. The token rule would have silently BROKEN the spelling that already worked while making my made-up case pass. The test now pins 'int id$' explicitly so the method fix cannot be bought by regressing the attribute one. A '+ptr() char*' control I had written was invented too and is gone.

The lesson matches the bead family already banked: a test that encodes its author's guess about the syntax is worse than no test, because it makes a regression look like a pass.

NEGATIVE CONTROL RUN: with the paren-adjacent branch disabled the test fails with
  left: [("count()", false, false, Some("$ int")), ("draw()", false, false, Some("* void"))]
which also shows the marker leaking into the RETURN TYPE, not merely being missed.

GATE, harness cargo test -j 2 -p fm-parser --lib: 545 passed, 0 failed, rch worker vmi1227854.
close_reason:
LANDED at 5f9920c8. See the bead body for the measured before/after, the two documented placements, and the invented-expectation near-miss.

Same commit-hygiene and gate caveats as bd-7i6b: committed as a reconstructed subset because a peer's uncommitted bd-1fw3 work was interleaved in the same file, and not re-gated in isolation because of the build freeze at the 58G floor.

The single most useful thing on this bead is the near-miss: my first fix would have made an INVENTED spelling work while silently breaking the documented one that already worked. It was caught only because the gate failed on a case I had written down before checking mermaid, and the honest response was to delete my invented cases rather than to make the parser accommodate them.

title: C4 BiRel renders as a plain undirected line, losing both arrowheads
description: USER-VISIBLE SEMANTIC LOSS. mermaid_parser.rs mapped the C4 macro BiRel(a, b, label) to ArrowType::Line, which the SVG renderer draws with NO markers on either end. C4 defines BiRel as a BIDIRECTIONAL relationship - an arrowhead on each end - so our output rendered it as a bare undirected segment: visually indistinguishable from a diagram that drew no relationship arrow at all, and carrying strictly less information than the Rel it exists to contrast with. FIX: map BiRel to ArrowType::DoubleArrow, the same variant the flowchart <--> form produces. That is not a cosmetic rename - fm-render-svg lib.rs:3322 gives DoubleArrow MARKER_START | MARKER_END, so the arrowheads reach the rendered output rather than only the IR. AN EXISTING TEST PINNED THE DEFECT: c4_birel_and_back_rel_map_to_expected_edges asserted edges[0].arrow == ArrowType::Line, i.e. it encoded the current behaviour rather than the specification. That assertion is STRENGTHENED to DoubleArrow, with the reason recorded at the line, and a CONTROL added so the fix cannot have simply made every C4 relationship bidirectional: a plain Rel must still produce a single-headed ArrowType::Arrow. NO GOLDEN MOVES - grep confirms no committed golden fixture uses BiRel (c4_basic exercises only Person, System, System_Ext and Rel), which is also why this went unnoticed: bd-g2g1 measured that 17 of the 21 C4 element macros have no byte golden behind them, and BiRel is one of them. GATE: cargo test -j 1 -p fm-parser --lib c4_birel_and_back_rel_map_to_expected_edges, 1 passed / 512 filtered, rch WORKER hz1 (104.8s), HARNESS 'cargo test -j 1 -p fm-parser --lib'.
close_reason: Fixed and gated: BiRel now maps to ArrowType::DoubleArrow, which the SVG renderer draws with MARKER_START|MARKER_END. The existing test that pinned ArrowType::Line was strengthened to the specification with a single-arrow control for plain Rel. No golden moves (no fixture uses BiRel). cargo test -j 1 -p fm-parser --lib c4_birel_and_back_rel_map_to_expected_edges, 1 passed / 512 filtered, rch WORKER hz1 (104.8s)

title: Sankey flows render at uniform width; ribbon thickness is not proportional to value
description:
Found by bd-iicc while writing a semantic guard for the sankey golden. The byte golden could never have caught this: the output is stable, it is just wrong.

MEASURED on crates/fm-cli/tests/golden/sankey_basic.svg at HEAD:

  fixture flow values : 100, 50, 75, 25, 120, 55, 50, 25   (max/min ratio 4.8x)
  rendered fm-edge stroke-widths : 1.80 x8, one distinct value
  rendered width ratio max/min : 1.0

Every flow is drawn at the same thickness regardless of magnitude.

WHY THIS IS A REAL DEFECT, not a style preference. Proportional ribbon width IS the sankey diagram - it is the entire reason the diagram type exists. A sankey whose flows are all the same width conveys no quantitative information and is a generic directed graph with sankey-shaped labels. mermaid-js renders sankey link thickness proportional to value, so this is also a cross-engine fidelity gap, and per AGENTS.md a renderer that mislays the meaning of its output is not fast, it is wrong.

WHAT IS ALREADY RIGHT, so nobody re-does it: parsing and topology are fine. All 8 flows are present, endpoints connect the right nodes, and the fixture's own conservation holds (Process X 175 in / 175 out, Y 50/50, Z 25/25). Node rects also render at varying heights, so some magnitude signal already reaches layout. The gap is specifically the LINK width.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, not prescriptive: the flow value is already in the IR, and edge rendering already emits a per-edge stroke-width attribute - it is currently a constant. Mapping value to width needs a scale with a sensible floor so a tiny flow stays visible, and a cap so one dominant flow does not swamp the canvas.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, observable:
1. For sankey_basic, rendered flow widths are a strictly monotonic function of flow value: the 120 flow is wider than the 100, which is wider than the 75, than the 55, than the 50s, than the 25s.
2. Equal values render equal widths (the two 50s, the two 25s) - this catches a scale keyed on edge index rather than value.
3. A minimum width floor keeps the smallest flow visible; state the floor in the test rather than leaving it implicit.
4. GOLDEN IMPACT: sankey_basic.svg will move. That is a legitimate GOLDEN-CHANGE and needs a semantic diff naming which widths changed and why the new ones are correct. Only the sankey fixture should move; if any other golden moves, the change reached further than intended.

TEST ALREADY WRITTEN AND WAITING: bd-iicc adds sankey_basic_flow_widths_are_proportional_to_values, currently #[ignore]d with a pointer to this bead. UN-IGNORING IT IS THIS BEAD'S ACCEPTANCE GATE - the assertion exists, is reviewable now, and turns green exactly when this is fixed. Do not weaken it to make it pass.
close_reason:
Fixed in 910f4348. Flow widths are now 20/10/15/5/24/11/10/5 for declared values 100/50/75/25/120/55/50/25 — exactly value/120*24, so a width ratio equals its value ratio.

ALL FOUR ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA MET:
1. Strictly monotonic in value — yes, linear.
2. Equal values render equal widths — the two 50s both render 10.0, the two 25s both 5.0. This is the criterion that rejects a scale keyed on edge index, and it is asserted in the test.
3. Minimum width floor — 1.5, stated in the code and asserted in the test.
4. Only sankey_basic.svg moved — verified by blessing and reading git status: exactly one file changed. Text, viewBox and every node rect are BYTE-IDENTICAL; only the eight ribbon widths differ. 15640 -> 15622 bytes.

THE TEST IS UN-IGNORED, which was this bead's stated acceptance gate.

IMPLEMENTATION: the flow amount was already in the IR — parse_sankey stores it as the edge LABEL — so no parser change was needed. sankey_flow_stroke_width normalises against the widest flow and returns None for anything that is not a numeric sankey flow, so every other diagram type and any malformed row keeps its arrow-derived width. That is what kept the other 36 goldens still.

FINDING THE SEAM TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS, recorded so the next person does not repeat it: edge width is decided in THREE places — render_edge (Element path), render_edge_into's arrow match, and render_edge_into's LABELED fast path. Sankey takes the third, because its edges always carry a label. Patching the first two changed nothing, and instrumenting proved render_edge is never called for sankey at all. All three now resolve width through the one helper, so they cannot drift.

BUG FOUND AND FIXED IN MY OWN TEST while landing this: splitting on '<path' without bounding each segment at its own '>' let the arrowhead <marker>'s inner path swallow the rest of the document and match a stroke-width belonging to elements far below — it reported 9 flows for 8 edges. Same unbounded-segment mistake I made earlier in the print-CSS guard, and the reason bd-iicc's guidance says to bound before searching.

Gates: cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast RC=0, all 40 binaries green; clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings RC=0; ubs no finding on changed lines.

title: A mistyped or unknown diagram-type header is interned as a graph node: 'flowchat LR' renders a box labelled flowchat_LR, and the parser already knows it is a typo
description:
MEASURED with the shipping binary (target/release/frankenmermaid, built 2026-08-15T22:18Z), node ids read from rendered SVG data-id and compared against a CONTROL, because the parse command's node_count has misreported for me before.

  input                          node ids                 control
  'flowchat LR' + A-->B-->C      flowchat_LR, A, B, C     ---
  'flowchart LR' + A-->B         A, B                     the same graph, correct header
  'notADiagramType' + A-->B      notADiagramType, A, B    ---

The unrecognised HEADER LINE becomes a node and is DRAWN: the SVG's visible text for the third case is exactly 'notADiagramType', 'A', 'B'.

⚠️ THE PARSER ALREADY KNOWS. validate on the typo case emits

  [parse][warning][mermaid/warn/unstructured-parse-warning] Fuzzy match: possible typo in
  diagram type declaration

So detection recognises the line as a mis-typed diagram-type declaration, warns the user about it, and then the very same line is interned as a graph node by the flowchart fallback. The two behaviours contradict each other: one says 'this is a header you typed wrong', the other says 'this is a node you asked for'.

USER-VISIBLE EFFECT: a one-letter typo does not produce an error, it produces a diagram containing a spurious box captioned with the typo. mermaid-js REJECTS both inputs outright, so a user moving from mermaid gets a silently different picture rather than the error they expect.

SAME FAMILY as bd-sq8p / bd-9x8r / bd-yf4r / bd-yrxu / bd-0di8 / bd-ij0f / bd-7oyz / bd-t2fp / bd-6r13 -- syntax interned as node identity -- but at the outermost level: the header rather than a statement. Every earlier member guarded a statement INSIDE a recognised diagram; nothing guards the line that failed to name the diagram.

NOT CLAIMED: that lenient parsing is wrong. FrankenMermaid deliberately accepts inputs mermaid rejects and warns instead, which for pie is done well -- 'a : notanumber' yields
  [parse][warning] Line 2: invalid pie slice value 'notanumber', defaulting to 0
That is lenient AND explicit, and it is the standard this bead asks the header path to meet. Recovering is fine; recovering by inventing a node the user never wrote is not.

NEGATIVE CASES a fix must handle:
  1. The correct header 'flowchart LR' must stay clean -- it is the control above and already is.
  2. The typo warning must SURVIVE the fix; removing the phantom must not remove the diagnosis.
  3. A node legitimately named after a diagram keyword must survive: 'flowchart LR' with a node
     'graph[Box]' must still declare graph.
  4. The first line of a HEADERLESS diagram that is genuinely a node must still be a node --
     content heuristics exist precisely because some inputs have no header, so the guard must key
     on 'this line was fuzzy-matched as a diagram-type declaration', which is information the
     parser already computed, not on a keyword list.

BUILD BUDGET: not fixed this turn. df -h /data reported 60G against the standing 60G floor for the whole turn, so no build could be started and a parser change cannot be gated. Evidence, controls and the fix contract are recorded here so the fix is a short job when disk allows.

Recomputed for ELF 08cca9e1, case flowchart_small_10:

  run                drift      floor     verdict  nullHW   cv% before/after
  cpu12 ..84185757   1.050140   1.024400  FAIL     0.0122   21.93 / 18.76
  cpu13 ..84198917   1.013775   1.036200  PASS     0.0181   16.27 / 14.61
  cpu12 ..83972865   1.038347   1.020000  FAIL     0.0092   11.84 /  5.15

title: Differential parse-acceptance oracle vs pinned mermaid-js: 24 constructs agree, 0 grammar divergences, 10 malformed inputs where we are lenient
description:
A BUILD-FREE CORRECTNESS ORACLE, usable on a frozen or contended turn. It asks only 'does each engine accept this input, and as what' -- no timing, so host load cannot invalidate it. Run against the pinned bundle sha 70137e77 with the shipping binary built 2026-08-15T22:18Z.

METHOD NOTE, and it is the opposite choice from the timing harness ON PURPOSE: mermaid.parse() is called WITHOUT mermaid.initialize(). initialize() registers DOMPurify hooks, which need a DOM and cut headless coverage to sequence+ER only. For a GRAMMAR question skipping it is valid and much wider -- flowchart, sequence, er, gantt, pie, gitgraph. It would NOT be valid for timing, where sanitisation is part of the work being compared.

WELL-FORMED CONSTRUCTS, 28 probed: 24 AGREE (both accept), 4 undecidable because headless mermaid needs a DOM (flow_double_circle, flow_subgraph_dir, flow_markdown_label, pie_title). ZERO cases where we reject what mermaid accepts. Constructs confirmed accepted by both include A & B --> C & D, chained arrows, edge ids (A e1@--> B), the e1@{animate} form, A@{shape:...}, linkStyle, click href, autonumber, activation +/-, par/and, critical/option, create participant, ER attribute keys and comments, gantt tickInterval/todayMarker/weekday/milestone, and pie showData.

⚠️ THREE APPARENT 'we accept what mermaid rejects' ROWS ARE ARTIFACTS, NOT FINDINGS: seq_box, git_cherry and git_tag fail in headless mermaid with 'Option is not defined' and 'Ro.sanitize is not a function'. Those are missing-DOM errors, not grammar rejections, and must not be reported as divergences. A headless incumbent can only be trusted where it fails for GRAMMAR reasons.

MALFORMED INPUTS, 13 probed. mermaid rejects and we accept in 10. That is by design -- lenient recovery -- and where checked it is done well: 'pie / a : notanumber' yields
  [parse][warning] Line 2: invalid pie slice value 'notanumber', defaulting to 0
lenient AND explicit. One case is NOT: the unrecognised diagram-type header becomes a node. Filed as bd-ec1t with controls.

⚠️⚠️ MY FIRST RUN OF THIS ORACLE REPORTED ALL 28 CONSTRUCTS AS 'WE REJECT WHAT MERMAID ACCEPTS' AND EVERY ROW WAS FALSE. The reject test was /error/i over the whole validate report -- and every report prints the header label 'Fail threshold: Error'. So the probe matched itself. A uniform verdict across every case is the tell: 28 defects of one shape is not a discovery, it is a broken instrument. The fix reads the '✓ Valid' verdict line and counts diagnostics by SEVERITY.

THIS IS THE THIRD SUBSTRING TRAP IN THIS CAMPAIGN: class 'inactive' contains 'active'; 'Node1' matches inside 'Node11'; and now a report body containing the word Error. Grepping a human-readable report for a severity WORD is never sound -- match the machine-readable field.

REUSABLE: scratchpad parse_diff.mjs and malformed.mjs. Worth re-running after parser changes and worth extending; it needs no build and no quiet host, which is exactly what makes it the right tool when the disk budget or host contention rules out everything else.

Produced one filed defect (bd-ec1t, unrecognised diagram-type header interned as a node) and one solid negative result: across 24 comparable well-formed constructs there is ZERO grammar divergence from pinned mermaid-js 11.15.0, and no case where we reject what mermaid accepts.

The negative result is the point. This seam has produced eleven defects, so it was worth asking whether ACCEPTANCE diverges too. It does not, which redirects effort away from grammar coverage and toward what the earlier beads already showed is the real weakness: what we do with input we accept -- interning syntax as node identity, dropping metadata the renderer needs, and silently recovering without saying so.

The most transferable part is the self-inflicted failure: the oracle's first run reported ALL 28 constructs as divergent because it grepped a human-readable report for the word 'error', and every report prints 'Fail threshold: Error'. PREFLIGHT RUN FOR THE FIRST TIME — this bead is BLOCKED. Recording it because nobody had checked, and a P4 sitting in `br ready` looks actionable until someone burns a session discovering it is not.

node scripts/ledger_preflight.mjs --lever "stochastic superoptimization search over hot layout kernel instruction sequences" --surface "crates/fm-layout hot kernels"
exits 2 with 8 covering REJECT rows.

As with bd-hcw3, the matches are largely keyword collisions on unrelated mechanisms (query_segment fast-path and friends) rather than anything about superoptimization. SEPARATELY, AND MORE USEFULLY: this bead is a research programme, not a bounded increment. "Stochastic superoptimization over hot layout kernels" presupposes (a) a kernel small and hot enough that instruction-level search pays, and (b) a verification oracle strong enough to trust a machine-found rewrite. This repo's own evidence argues against (a) right now — the measured frontier has been algorithmic and allocation-shaped (byte_lines, CSR adjacency, obstacle indexing, single-pass barycenter), not instruction-shaped, and the crossing-counter rewrites that WERE instruction-shaped are recorded as REJECTED or measurement-invalid. If it is ever picked up, the honest entry condition is a profile showing a specific kernel above some meaningful self-time threshold — not a general belief that superoptimization is powerful. Without that, the preflight block is the least of its problems.

title: ER attributes never reach terminal output at any viewport, while class members do
description:
MEASURED. erDiagram with CUSTOMER { string name PK / int age } parses to an IR where CUSTOMER carries 2 members, and the terminal renders the entity NAME only. name, age and PK are all absent at 100x40, 200x60 AND 400x120 - size-independent, so it is not the viewport ceiling of bd-8tsw.

CONTROL that makes this ER-specific rather than a terminal-wide limitation: a classDiagram with class Alpha { +String name / +run() } renders Alpha, name AND run in the terminal at the same settings. The terminal has compartment rendering (overlay_class_compartments); ER simply never got it.

ROOT CAUSE: the identifier "members" does not appear anywhere in crates/fm-render-term/src/renderer.rs. IrNode.members is populated only for ER entities, and the terminal node path draws the label and stops. fm-render-svg draws a name header, a divider and one row per attribute; the terminal draws the box and the name.

WHY EXISTING GATES MISSED IT: the declared-text terminal gate's er case asserts CUSTOMER, ORDER and places - the entity and relationship names - and never an ATTRIBUTE name. The SVG feature-parity gate does cover er_attribute_pk and er_attribute_comment, but only against SVG output. Neither gate looked for attribute text in the terminal.

FOUND BY probing a class I had not tested: features whose effect is TEXTUAL, honoured by SVG and dropped by the terminal. Two other members of that class turned up in the same probe and are separate from this bead: class cardinality ("1" --> "many") renders identically in the terminal, and so does er PK - the latter being a symptom of this bead rather than its own defect.

FIX: mirror overlay_class_compartments for ER members. No layout change is needed - er_compartment_dimensions already sizes the entity box to hold its rows, so the box is big enough today and only the text is missing.
close_reason: done

title: GPU text quads use a global font size while layout already resolves it per text
description:
THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE PATTERN, and the pattern is the point: gpu_plan carries a field that exists,
has the right type and sits at the right offset, and is filled with a CONSTANT while the raster path
resolves the real value. A struct check, an ABI guard and the compiler all pass; only a test that
asks what VALUE arrives can tell the difference.

  a3157251  node stroke width  -- shader had a global STROKE_WIDTH = 1.5      FIXED
  58564713  label colour       -- every quad got DEFAULT_LABEL_RGBA           FIXED
  THIS      label font size    -- every quad sized from DEFAULT_FONT_SIZE_PX  OPEN

MECHANISM, traced rather than guessed. gpu_plan.rs:621-622 computes the glyph advance and half
height from DEFAULT_FONT_SIZE_PX (14.0) for every run:

    let advance = DEFAULT_FONT_SIZE_PX * CHAR_ADVANCE_RATIO;
    let half_height = DEFAULT_FONT_SIZE_PX * 0.5;

So `style a font-size:28px` and a classDef carrying font-size reach the Canvas2D path -- renderer.rs
:584 reads text.font_size per text, and node_font_size.rs has four tests including a malformed-value
control -- and are discarded on the GPU path. Every label renders at 14px whatever the author wrote.

WHY THIS ONE IS NOT A ONE-LINE FIX like its two siblings, which is why it is filed rather than
landed. The colour fix worked because the node index was already in scope and resolve_node_text_color
takes it. The resolved font size does NOT live on the node: it is on the layout TEXT primitive
(fm-layout RenderText.font_size, lib.rs:2541), and gpu_plan builds its runs from layout.nodes plus
ir.labels and never consults the text primitives at all. RenderText carries `source: RenderSource`,
so the association exists -- the work is routing the GPU text pass through those primitives instead
of re-deriving label placement from node bounds, which also decides whether the GPU pass inherits the
alignment and baseline it currently ignores.

⚠️ IT IS ALSO NOT JUST A NUMBER. advance and half_height set the quad geometry, so a per-run font
size changes the atlas cell mapping and the run width used to centre the label. A fix that scales the
quads without revisiting GlyphAtlasPlan::for_texts (built once at DEFAULT_GLYPH_CELL_PX) will render
large text blurry rather than wrong, which is the kind of defect that survives review.

SUGGESTED ORDER: route the text pass through the layout text primitives first and assert the
existing colour test still passes, THEN take the font size, so the routing change and the sizing
change fail separately.
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED (54d5f637) — AND THE RECOMMENDATION IN THIS BEAD WAS WRONG. Correcting it here because
acting on it would have produced a large refactor that delivered nothing.

WHAT I WROTE: "the resolved font size ... is on the layout TEXT primitive (fm-layout
RenderText.font_size, lib.rs:2541), and gpu_plan ... never consults the text primitives at all ...
the work is routing the GPU text pass through those primitives".

WHAT IS TRUE: every font_size in build_render_scene is a hardcoded constant — 14.0 at lib.rs:2986
and 3010, 12.0 at 3036 and 3061. The scene NEVER carries a declared size. Routing the GPU text pass
through it would have moved the pass onto a different source of the same wrong number, at the cost
of a refactor, and the tests would have passed because the default is what they compare against.

WHERE THE VALUE ACTUALLY LIVES: resolve_declared_node_font(ir, node_index), which the Canvas2D pass
has used all along (renderer.rs:3389, reached from the node loop at :2048). node_index is already in
scope where gpu_plan builds its runs, so this was the SAME one-resolver shape as stroke width
(a3157251), label colour (58564713) and opacity (a2b268c5) — the fourth field whose value was
available at the exact site that ignored it.

HOW I GOT IT WRONG: I read a struct field name. `RenderText.font_size` exists, is an f32, and is
exactly what a resolved size would look like. Nothing about the declaration says "always 14.0"
except reading its assignments, which I did not do before filing. A field that COULD carry the value
is not a field that DOES — the same mistake as a `color` field faithfully populated with a constant,
which is the defect this family keeps producing.

THE BEAD WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE ATLAS, and that half stood: enlarged quads sampling a 32px cell render
BLURRY rather than wrong, which survives review because the geometry is correct and only the raster
is soft. The cell now scales with the largest declared label (32px cell for a 14px glyph is the
headroom ratio that scales), capped at 256 so a pathological declaration cannot ask a backend for an
enormous texture. Smaller labels sample DOWN from a sharp cell, the harmless direction.

Tests assert both halves plus both controls: a 32px declaration enlarges the quad AND the cell,
while an undeclared diagram keeps the default cell so the atlas is not enlarged for every diagram on
the strength of one styled node. 84 passed, clippy -D warnings exit 0.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CLOSED BY 54d5f637. Per-node font size reaches the GPU text quads, with the glyph atlas cell scaled
to the largest declared label so big text is rasterised sharp rather than upscaled blurry.

⚠️ AND THE RECOMMENDATION IN THIS BEAD WAS WRONG, corrected in the comment above: the resolved size
is NOT on the layout text primitive (every font_size in build_render_scene is a hardcoded 14.0 or
12.0). Routing the GPU text pass through the scene, which this bead recommended, would have been a
refactor delivering the same wrong number. The value comes from resolve_declared_node_font(ir,
node_index), available where the plan already sits.

title: requirement id: and text: are parsed into the IR and never rendered, so the requirement's own statement is invisible
description:
Found by bd-iicc round 5, the semantic-guard sweep. This is the defect class a byte golden is blindest to: nothing is misplaced and nothing is malformed, content simply never appears, and a hash of the output cannot miss what was never there to change.

WHAT IS LOST. A requirement diagram's `id:` is its traceability key and its `text:` is the requirement itself — the sentence the diagram exists to record. golden/requirement_basic declares both on both requirements:
    AuthReq   id: REQ-001   text: Users must authenticate
    LoginReq  id: REQ-002   text: Support OAuth2 login
Neither string appears anywhere in the rendered SVG. The three rows actually drawn are the type header, the name, and `Risk: … | Verify: …`.

WHERE IT IS DROPPED — and it is NOT the parser. crates/fm-parser/src/mermaid_parser.rs:3908 parses all four block fields and stores them:
    "id"           -> meta.req_id
    "text"         -> meta.text
    "risk"         -> meta.risk
    "verifymethod" -> meta.verify_method
`IrRequirementNodeMeta` (crates/fm-core/src/lib.rs:4550) carries all four. The SVG renderer (crates/fm-render-svg/src/lib.rs:9389-9505) then builds its metadata row from `req_meta.risk` and `req_meta.verify_method` ONLY and never mentions the other two. `rg req_id` across fm-render-svg, fm-render-term, fm-render-canvas and fm-layout returns exactly one hit, and it is a test fixture. So both fields are parsed, held in the IR, read by nothing, and dropped on the floor.

ACCEPTANCE GATE, named and populated: remove the `#[ignore]` from
    requirement_id_and_text_reach_the_output   (crates/fm-cli/tests/golden_svg_test.rs)
and it must pass. It currently FAILS naming all four missing values against the rows actually drawn — verified under `--ignored`, so it is a real specification and not a stub. The expected values are READ FROM THE FIXTURE rather than restated in the test, so the guard cannot drift from what the diagram declares, and a fixture that declared no `id:`/`text:` at all is a hard error rather than a quiet pass.

ORDERING CONSTRAINT — read this before starting. Rendering these two fields adds two more rows to a box that is ALREADY too small for the rows it has: bd-jnc1 records that `compute_node_size` never measures requirement metadata at all, so LoginReq's existing `Risk … | Verify …` row already spills 15.16px past each side. Fix bd-jnc1 first, or the new id/text rows will overflow with it. `text:` is free-form prose and can be long, so the sizing pass will likely need to WRAP it the way `c4_description_height` wraps a C4 description, not merely widen for it.

SCOPE NOTE: this bead is about the two fields never reaching the picture. It does not prejudge the row FORMAT — whether they render as `Id: REQ-001` / `Text: …` rows in mermaid's style or fold into the existing metadata line is a rendering decision. The gate is that the declared information is visible.
close_reason: Landed a656acc4. id: and text: now render as their own rows (classes fm-req-id / fm-req-text) between the name and the risk row, which is where the pinned mermaid-js 11.15.0 requirement renderer puts them. Both the streaming fast writer and the Element slow path edited together; requirement_node_streaming_matches_slow_render covers a node with all five fields. Sized by the bd-jnc1 pass (requirement_row_dimensions) and hashed into node_size_cache_key, so a stale size cannot put them back outside the box. WIDENED, NOT WRAPPED — the bead suggested wrapping like c4_description_height, but the incumbent draws each row unwrapped and grows the box to its bbox; recorded at the code. GATE: requirement_id_and_text_reach_the_output un-ignored and passing, with requirement_rows_stay_inside_their_node_box still passing so the new rows are contained, not just present. Plus requirement_box_holds_its_id_and_text_rows (20 growing text: strings + cache-key coverage). GOLDEN-CHANGE: viewBox height 623.5 -> 652.5, layout checksum 925e63ce -> fbaa0703, height 543.5 -> 572.5; width unchanged (metadata row was already widest); no other case blessed. REMAINING DIVERGENCE, out of scope by the bead's own scope note: mermaid splits Risk and Verification into two rows, we keep Risk: X | Verify: Y. cargo test --workspace 0 failures; clippy -D warnings clean.

title: GPU dashed edges restart their pattern at every bend: no dash phase on the segment
description:
MECHANISM, read rather than inferred. gpu_plan builds edge segments with
`for points in edge.points.windows(2)`, so a routed edge with N points becomes N-1 GpuEdgeSegment
instances. Each carries the SAME `dash: [on, off]` and there is no phase field, so every segment
starts its pattern from zero.

CONSEQUENCE: on a dotted edge with bends, the dash pattern restarts at each vertex. The raster and
SVG paths draw one continuous path with a single stroke-dasharray, where the pattern runs unbroken
around every corner. So a `-.->` edge with two bends looks different on the GPU path from the other
two surfaces -- dashes bunching or gapping at the corners rather than marching evenly.

NOT VISIBLE TODAY because nothing executes these buffers on a GPU; this is a defect in the PLAN, and
it will become a visible one the moment a backend consumes it. Filed now because the plan is what a
backend will trust.

⚠️ SEVERITY IS LOW AND THE SHAPE IS FAMILIAR: it is the same family as the five styling channels
(a3157251, 58564713, a2b268c5, 54d5f637, f5769ac8) -- the GPU path carrying a value the raster path
resolves differently -- except here the field is ABSENT rather than constant.

FIX SHAPE:
  1. `dash_phase: f32` on GpuEdgeSegment, accumulating the distance travelled along the edge so far
     (modulo the pattern period) as segments are emitted.
  2. An @location(6) Float32 attribute and a matching WGSL member in EDGE_WGSL.
  3. EDGE_WGSL offsetting its dash lookup by the phase.

⚠️ STEP 2 IS NOW SAFE IN A WAY IT WAS NOT YESTERDAY. every_shader_and_its_buffer_layout_agree
(171f0cdd) covers the EDGE pair as of today -- before that it checked the node pair only, so an edge
attribute added without the matching WGSL member would have passed the gate. Whoever takes this gets
a failing test if the three descriptions drift, which is the whole reason to add the field rather
than special-case it.

STEP 3 IS THE UNVERIFIABLE ONE: there is no naga on this host and no GPU, so the shader change can be
checked for ABI agreement but not for correctness. Say so on whatever lands.

RELATED: bd-l3nsf (node BORDER dash) is a different and harder problem -- an SDF border has no
perimeter parameter at all, whereas an edge segment is a line and its along-length is already the
projection the ribbon shader computes.
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DONE in 59578a01. dash_phase on GpuEdgeSegment = summed length of prior segments; EDGE_WGSL takes it at @location(6) as a flat varying and adds it to arc_length before the modulo, so the pattern marches unbroken through bends.

Two things worth recording for whoever picks up the next GPU bead:

1. The ABI half is mutation-PROVEN, not assumed. Dropping @location(6) from the WGSL while keeping the buffer attribute FAILS every_shader_and_its_buffer_layout_agree. But the older edge-specific test the_edge_shaders_declare_the_fields_the_buffers_carry PASSES under that same mutation - it does not check locations. The generalised gate (171f0cdd) is the one carrying the weight here.

2. The behavioural test guards its own vacuity. The accumulator is trivially correct on a single-segment edge (every phase 0.0), so the test asserts the fixture BENDS; without that line it would pass with the field deleted.

Step 3 (shader arithmetic executing correctly on a device) remains unverifiable here - no naga, no GPU. The change is a constant added before an existing modulo, which is as reviewable by eye as this gets, but it is NOT execution-verified and should not be recorded as such.

title: Terminal and ascii output coverage sweep: 20 diagram types x 2 formats, found the -f ascii format does nothing
description:
The SVG path is what every golden and audit exercises; -f term and -f ascii are separate renderers. The ledger records a family where a whole feature was drawn in SVG and silently absent elsewhere (gantt: no time axis, no section band, no section label, because an early return skipped loops layout had already filled).

METHOD: for each diagram type, render to term and to ascii and ask whether the labels the user wrote are present, plus an 'ink' count of non-whitespace, non-box-drawing characters so an empty canvas cannot pass as a render.

RESULT: 20 diagram types x 2 formats = 40 renders. Every type draws ink and almost all labels appear.

title: 21 of 32 ER cardinality operators were missing and mangled entity names
description:
TWENTY-ONE of mermaid's thirty-two ER cardinality operators were missing from ER_OPERATORS, and the
omission was SILENT AND DESTRUCTIVE rather than merely unsupported - because the same table ends
with bare `--` and `..` fallbacks.

MECHANISM: find_operator for ER scans left to right and takes the longest operator matching AT each
position. For a missing combination - `A }o--o| B` - nothing matches at the `}`, the scan walks on
and matches the bare `--` in the middle, and parse_er_relationship then splits the endpoints THERE:

    left_raw  = "A }o"      ->  normalised into a mangled entity name
    right_raw = "o| B"      ->  likewise

So the diagram gains entities the author never wrote, the real entities go unconnected, and the
recorded er_notation is `--` with the cardinality thrown away. A missing combination does not fail
loudly; it quietly redraws the diagram.

mermaid's grammar is a product: LEFT in {||, |o, }|, }o} x LINE in {--, ..} x RIGHT in {||, o|, |{,
o{} = 32. Twelve were listed. Every missing one PARSES in the pinned bundle - spot-checked }o--o|,
|o--|{, ||--o|, }|--o{, |o..o{, ||..o{.

FIXED: the grid is now complete (35 entries: the 12 that were there, 21 added, plus the two bare
fallbacks kept LAST). Generated from the product rather than hand-written, so extending a cardinality
token set means editing the sets.

`o|--|{` is KEPT even though `o|` is not a left-hand token in mermaid's grammar. It predates this
bead; removing it would be a behaviour change nobody asked for, not a fix.

TEST is generative over the whole grid rather than a handful of examples, because the defect was an
omission and a list of examples cannot catch the next one. The load-bearing assertion is on the
entity NAMES: a mangled parse still produces two nodes and one edge, so counting alone would pass on
the exact defect this covers.

title: Publishing the worker render entry point needs 19.6KB of gzip headroom the wasm budget does not have
description:
BLOCKS a published-artifact refresh, not the source feature. 3c0926ba (bd-2u0.6) added
`workerHandleMessage`, the wasm entry point for the worker render protocol. It works, is tested,
and passes `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. It is NOT in the vendored `pkg/` because
regenerating the package fails build-wasm.sh's own size gate.

MEASURED, same script, same gzip level (`gzip -c`, the script's default level, NOT -9):

  committed pkg/frankenmermaid_bg.wasm   548,767 bytes gzipped   (4,193 under budget)
  rebuilt with workerHandleMessage       568,377 bytes gzipped   (15,417 OVER budget)
  budget (MAX_GZIP_BYTES)                552,960 bytes
  cost attributable to the change        +19,610 bytes gzipped, raw 1,307,199 -> 1,351,148

Attribution is not guesswork: the committed artifact was rebuilt by a peer earlier the same day
(764e8994) and is under budget, so the overage arrived with this change.

I DID NOT RAISE THE BUDGET. Editing MAX_GZIP_BYTES to land a change is gate self-weakening, and the
gate is working exactly as intended here — the artifact had ~4KB of headroom and the feature wants
20KB. I also did not commit the oversized artifact: `pkg/` is gitignored-yet-tracked, so an
oversized build sitting in the working tree would be invisible to `git status` and could be swept
into someone else's commit. The four tracked pkg/ files were restored to their committed bytes and
verified identical to HEAD.

ONE HYPOTHESIS TESTED AND FALSIFIED, recorded so nobody repeats it. I suspected the cost was the
`Deserialize` derive on `WorkerRenderResponse` instantiating a deserializer for `Vec<Diagnostic>`,
since the wasm module only ever SERIALIZES responses. Gating that derive to
`any(not(target_arch = "wasm32"), test)` changed the artifact by THREE BYTES gzipped and left the
raw size byte-identical at 1,351,148 — the unused deserializer was already dead-code-eliminated by
LTO plus wasm-opt. I reverted that change rather than keep dead complexity behind a comment my own
measurement contradicted.

REMAINING SUSPECT, unmeasured, do not treat as established: `worker_handle_message_js` calls
`serde_json::from_str::<WorkerRenderMessage>`, which may instantiate serde_json's PARSER in the wasm
module for the first time. fm-core and fm-layout depend on serde_json unconditionally, but if
nothing wasm-reachable previously deserialized, the parser would not have been linked. Testing this
costs one build: replace the JSON-text entry point with a `serde_wasm_bindgen` (JsValue) one and
re-measure. If that recovers the 20KB, it is also a defensible design — a plain JS object is
structured-clone-safe, so the protocol keeps its property without a JSON parser in the module. The
Rust-side `WorkerRenderMessage`/`WorkerRenderResponse` types and the String-based
`handle_worker_message` would stay for native use and tests either way.

DECISIONS FOR THE OWNER, none of which are one lane's to make:
  (a) Spend the headroom: raise the budget deliberately, with the reason recorded, the way the
      500K -> 540K raise on 2026-07-24 was.
  (b) Buy the space back: the JsValue entry point above, or find 20KB elsewhere.
  (c) Do not publish it yet: leave the export source-only until the worker script (bd-2u0.6 item 1)
      actually needs it. Costs nothing today; the source is already tested.
This interacts with bd-jj8d criterion 1 (whether pkg/ is vendored at all) — under "stop vendoring,
build in CI", the budget question changes shape entirely.

NOTE for whoever refreshes pkg/ next: scripts/check-wasm-freshness.mjs passes (4/4) against the
CURRENT committed artifact even though it lacks `workerHandleMessage`, because the check is
behavioral by design — it pins render fixes, not the export surface. That is the right design for
what it was built for, and it means a MISSING EXPORT is not something it can detect.
close_reason: Worker-boundary parser-elimination hypothesis is invalid: serde_json parsing is already wasm-reachable through runtime config.

I ran the attribution the bead priced at "one build". It took three, each 2.7-15s with warm deps, so

  DOT `splines=curved|spline|true`                        -> EdgeRouting::Spline

title: Wall-clock time limit in egraph_crossing saturation makes its output load-dependent before it is ever wired in
description:
FOUND while excluding mechanism (b) of bd-ryxg. Not a live defect today; a trap set for whoever
adopts the module.

crates/fm-layout/src/egraph_crossing.rs builds its saturation runner with

  .with_time_limit(std::time::Duration::from_millis(config.time_limit_ms))   (line 368)

and SaturationConfig::time_limit_ms is chosen from the graph shape
(10 * layer_count, capped at 500, line 286). A wall-clock stop condition means the crossing result
this module returns is a function of HOW BUSY THE HOST IS: on a loaded box the runner stops earlier,
returns a different e-graph, and therefore a different layer ordering. That is the same defect class
as bd-9a1t (output as a function of measured wall time), which the campaign has already paid for
once in false byte-divergence during cross-engine equivalence runs.

REACHABILITY, checked rather than assumed. Nothing in the layout pipeline calls it:
  rg 'egraph_crossing' --type rust crates/
    crates/fm-layout/src/lib.rs:2568  pub mod egraph_crossing;
    crates/fm-layout/benches/crossing_minimization.rs:12  use fm_layout::egraph_crossing::{...}
So it is compiled, publicly exported, and exercised only by a bench. No rendered output depends on
it today, which is exactly why this is cheap to fix now and expensive to fix later.

NOTE the module already has a test named fault_deterministic_output_across_runs, which passes. It
cannot catch this: repeated runs on the same quiet host stay inside the time limit, so the limit
never binds. Determinism tests that do not STARVE the budget are blind to budget-driven divergence —
the same vacuity that bd-9a1t's probe 2 control was written to catch, and did catch.

FIX SHAPE (do not just delete the limit — it is there to bound worst-case work): make the stop
condition a COUNTED one. egg runners accept iteration and node limits; iter_limit and node_limit are
already in SaturationConfig. Derive the bound from graph size alone and drop with_time_limit, or
keep it strictly as a safety valve that also fails the result closed (i.e. falls back to the greedy
result deterministically) rather than returning a partially-saturated e-graph whose contents depend
on scheduling.

PROBE TO CLOSE: a test that runs saturation twice on the same input with two very different
time_limit_ms values (e.g. 1ms and 1000ms) and requires either identical output, or an explicit
documented fallback verdict in the short-budget arm — not a silently different ordering.

BLOCKED IN PRACTICE at filing time: crates/fm-layout/src/lib.rs and its module tree are under an
exclusive Agent Mail lease held by StormyFalcon until 2026-08-15T15:08:41Z.
close_reason: Fixed by 57b22564. Wall-clock stop condition no longer shapes the ordering: time_limit_ms -> wall_clock_valve_ms fixed at WALL_CLOCK_VALVE_MS=30_000 for every preset (no shape-derived clock budget), and saturate_layer fails the result CLOSED to the input ordering when the valve fires instead of extracting from a partially-explored e-graph. BudgetType::TimeLimit now documents 'abandoned, no optimization applied'. PROBE (named in this bead): wall_clock_valve_never_silently_reshapes_the_ordering, passing, in cargo test -p fm-layout --lib 478 passed / 0 failed on the remote fleet. NEGATIVE CONTROL: with the fail-closed branch disabled the mid-search case returns [0,1,2,8,7,6,5,4,3] against an input of [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8] -- a third ordering, neither input nor optimum, i.e. the defect exactly as filed. Source restored byte-identically. THE FIRST PROBE WAS VACUOUS AND THE CONTROL CAUGHT IT: a zero-length valve stops the runner before any rewriting, so the e-graph holds only the input and even the OLD code could only extract the input back. The discriminating case is a valve firing PART WAY THROUGH -- nine fully-inverted nodes, counted budget lifted out of the way, 20ms valve -- and it carries its own control (egraph_nodes > input len) so it fails loudly rather than passing free if the valve ever fires before the search moves. Config assertions that pinned the clock now pin the counted budgets; stated in the commit because it looks like relaxation and is not. GATES: clippy -p fm-layout --all-targets -D warnings clean, rustfmt --check clean, ubs exit 0. Pushed to main and master.

title: estimate_width: one non-ASCII char costs the whole label its width table (docs_site_50, the worst render ratio)
description:
TARGETS THE RIGHT ROW. Per the correction banked at 7697529c, sorting the ledger by measured_ratio selects rows whose arm does no rendering; the worst ratio this engine ACTUALLY RENDERS AT is docs_site_50 at 434.107779x (50 diagrams, 940 nodes / 902 edges, 5.887478 ms vs mermaid-js 2,555.800 ms). The ledger describes that workload as flowchart-dominated with 'escaping/non-ASCII labels'.

THE DEFECT, in crates/fm-core/src/font_metrics.rs estimate_width (:317). The ASCII fast path is gated on the WHOLE STRING:

    if self.config.preset != FontPreset::Monospace && text.is_ascii() { ...table... }
    text.chars().map(|c| self.char_width(c)).sum()

So a label like 'Cafe' with one accented char — three ASCII characters and one non-ASCII — sends EVERY character down the classify() match chain instead of the precomputed multiplier table. One non-ASCII byte costs the whole label its fast path, and char_width also re-tests the monospace preset once per character inside the loop. That is exactly the docs_site_50 label shape, measured across 940 node labels.

⚠️ REFUTED FIRST, so the sweep is not mistaken for a guess: I checked the ESCAPE path before this one, since 'escaping' is the other half of that workload's description and escape is ~19% of flowchart render self-time. write_escaped_attr and write_escaped_text (fm-render-svg/src/attributes.rs:490, :524) are CLEAN — both fast paths test only for specific ASCII bytes, so a non-ASCII byte is never in the special set and mixed-script text bulk-copies through the fast path unpenalized. Escaping is not the non-ASCII cost; measurement is.

THE FIX IS BIT-IDENTICAL BY CONSTRUCTION, which matters because node sizes derive from this number and every committed golden encodes the resulting geometry. ASCII_WIDTH_MULT (:222) is BUILT at compile time as classify(i as char).multiplier() for every i < 128, so for an ASCII char the table and the match chain are the same f32 by definition, not by coincidence. Keep the pure-ASCII bytes() path unchanged (it is the vectorizable shape), and give the mixed-script case a chars() loop that uses the table for ASCII chars and classify() only for the rest. Every term stays avg * multiplier(c) and the terms stay summed left-to-right over chars() in order, so the f32 accumulation sequence is unchanged and no golden can move. The monospace preset test is hoisted out of the loop as a free side effect: it cannot change per character.

CODE AND TESTS ARE WRITTEN, NOT APPLIED — the disk hard stop (42G) forbids any build, so nothing is gated. Parked at scratchpad/lever_mixed_script_width.py, applies in one shot, gate with cargo test -j 1 -p fm-core --lib.

THE TESTS ASSERT BITS, NOT EPSILON, because a one-ulp drift here is a corpus-wide golden diff: to_bits() equality against a per-character classify() reference over eight strings covering a combining accent, mostly-ASCII-with-accents (the docs_site_50 shape), pure CJK, leading non-ASCII, alternating runs, pure ASCII, empty, and a single non-ASCII char. Plus a monospace control, because monospace is a different rule — every char is one avg_char_width including full-width ones — and folding it into the width table would silently widen every CJK label in a monospace diagram.

⚠️ A TRAP I HIT WRITING THAT CONTROL, worth knowing: I first wrote the monospace expectation as avg * count. Repeated f32 addition and a single multiply are NOT bit-equal in general, so a bits assertion written that way fails on correct code. The reference has to mirror how the implementation accumulates. Corrected before parking.

NOT A MEASURED WIN. This is strictly-less-work with a structural bit-identity argument; whether it moves docs_site_50 needs the head-to-head harness. Its value should be judged against the ~19% escape / ~34% num-format render floor already recorded for flowcharts, and against how many of the 940 labels are actually mixed-script — which is itself worth counting from the corpus before certifying.
close_reason: Landed. estimate_width's ASCII fast path was gated on the WHOLE string being ASCII, so a label like 'Café' sent every character down the classify() match chain. Pure-ASCII keeps the vectorizable bytes() path unchanged; mixed-script now uses the table for ASCII chars and classify() only for the rest, with the monospace preset test hoisted out of the loop. BIT-IDENTICAL BY CONSTRUCTION: ASCII_WIDTH_MULT is built at compile time as classify(i as char).multiplier() for i<128, and the terms are still summed left-to-right over chars() in order. Gates on rch worker hz2: cargo test -j 1 -p fm-core --lib 420 passed 0 failed; golden_layout_test failing set EXACTLY the pre-existing four (all_node_shapes, cycle_braid, cycle_ladder, fuzzy_keyword_recovery), i.e. no golden moved, which is the empirical confirmation of the bit-identity argument. Sized at 10.6% of docs_site_50 labels (103 of 971), recovering 1,214 of 1,377 characters in those labels to the table — real but small, which is why this was P3. NOT a measured speedup; loadavg 15.29 16.85 23.16 at gate time, and no certification run was attempted.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SIZED, AND IT DOWNGRADES THIS BEAD. Counted with node over scripts/headtohead/corpus.mjs for the pinned docs_site_50 item (gen docs_site, count 50, seed 20260728) — no build. 50 diagrams, 971 extracted labels: 868 pure-ASCII, 103 mixed-script (10.6%). Inside those 103 labels there are 1,377 characters, of which 1,214 (88.2%) are ASCII. So the fix moves 1,214 characters from the classify() match chain onto the table lookup and leaves 163 on classify(); it does not touch the other 868 labels, which already take the byte path.

I filed this bead off the ledger's description of docs_site_50 as having 'escaping/non-ASCII labels', which reads as though non-ASCII dominates the workload. IT DOES NOT — 89.4% of labels are pure ASCII and already fast. The lever is still real, still strictly-less-work and still bit-identical by construction, but it is a ~1,200-character improvement inside a 5.887478 ms whole-job sample rather than a structural win. Priority lowered from P1 to P3 accordingly. It should NOT be the first thing a scarce build slot is spent on.

⚠️ The label count is approximate: a bracket/paren/brace/': text' regex yields 971 against the certified row's 940 nodes / 902 edges, so it over-approximates node labels and under-approximates edge labels. The 10.6% SHARE is the load-bearing number and is insensitive to that, because the same regex selects both classes.

Banked in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md. No timing claimed — this sizes a candidate, it does not measure one.

title: architecture-beta '<-->' renders as a bare line, losing both arrowheads
description: THIRD INSTANCE OF THE SAME SEAM, found by the arrow-expectation audit that follows the shape audit. parse_architecture_edge mapped '<-->' to ArrowType::Line, which fm-render-svg draws with NO markers on either end. In mermaid's architecture-beta '<-->' is a BIDIRECTIONAL edge: 'api <--> db' says these two talk in both directions, and a bare undirected segment states nothing about direction at all. Worse, it made the bidirectional form indistinguishable from the plain '--' in the very same operator table, and left it carrying strictly less information than the one-way '-->' it exists to contrast with. AN EXISTING TEST PINNED THE DEFECT, exactly as in bd-e29r: architecture_reverse_and_bidirectional_edges_map_cleanly asserted edges[1].arrow == ArrowType::Line, encoding current behaviour rather than the specification. FIX: map '<-->' to ArrowType::DoubleArrow, the variant flowchart '<-->' already produces and which fm-render-svg gives MARKER_START | MARKER_END, so the heads reach the rendered output rather than only the IR. Its 'reverse' flag also goes false — a bidirectional edge has no source to swap, and leaving it true silently reversed the stored endpoints for no visible gain. The assertion is STRENGTHENED to DoubleArrow with the reason recorded at the line, and the '<--' row directly above is the control: a one-way edge must stay single-headed, so the fix cannot have made every architecture edge bidirectional. NO GOLDEN MOVES: grep over crates/fm-cli/tests/golden/*.mmd finds no architecture fixture using '<-->' (the only '<-->' in the corpus is the flowchart one in all_edge_types, a different code path). GATE: cargo test -j 1 -p fm-parser --lib architecture — 8 passed, 515 filtered — rch WORKER vmi1227854 (159.9s), HARNESS 'cargo test -j 1 -p fm-parser --lib'. SEAM STATUS: bd-e29r was C4 BiRel, bd-8yj9 was class '<..', this is architecture '<-->'. All three are the same shape — a direction-bearing operator collapsed onto a variant that draws fewer markers — and all three were pinned by a test that asserted the buggy value.
close_reason: Landed. '<-->' -> ArrowType::DoubleArrow in parse_architecture_edge; pinning assertion strengthened with the '<--' single-head control. Gate 8 passed on rch worker vmi1227854.

title: Edges are routed through the middle of unrelated node boxes: 30 cases across 5 committed goldens, up to 33px deep
description:
EDGES ARE ROUTED THROUGH THE MIDDLE OF UNRELATED NODES. An edge that passes
through a node box reads as connecting to it, so the picture asserts a
relationship the source never declared. Same family as bd-h9gx and bd-5wbp: the
diagram still looks well-formed, which is what makes it expensive.

MEASURED ON THE COMMITTED GOLDENS, 30 cases across 5 files:

  cycle_feedback.svg   16   worst: edge 2  (Process2 -> Process3) enters 'ErrorHandler' 33.2px
  cycle_ladder.svg      5   worst: edge 20 (L5 -> L2)             enters 'R4'           33.2px
  cycle_scc_heavy.svg   4   worst: edge 12 (A2 -> B1)             enters 'B4'           32.7px
  state_composite.svg   3   worst: edge 5  (Idle -> Processing)   enters 'TaskB'        29.9px
  cycle_braid.svg       2   worst: edge 5  (T3 -> M3)             enters 'B3'           18.7px

"Depth" is the shortest distance from the deepest curve sample to any box edge,
so 33.2px inside a 66.5px-tall node box is the CENTRE of that node, not a
clipped corner. These are not near-misses.

HOW IT WAS MEASURED, because a crude version of this probe over-reports and I
want the next person to be able to reproduce it rather than trust it:
  - Bezier segments are evaluated as TRUE CUBICS at 60 samples each. Treating a
    C segment by its chord is wrong in both directions and inflated my own first
    pass from 30 to 37.
  - Control points are NOT treated as path vertices. That was the other half of
    the same first-pass error.
  - An edge's OWN endpoints are excluded, resolved from the edge group's
    <title>A points to B</title> and matched against each node's data-id.
  - Edges with NO <title> are SKIPPED rather than counted, because endpoints
    cannot be excluded without one. This is why timeline_basic's 7 apparent hits
    are not in the total: they are unverifiable, not innocent. Someone should
    check timeline separately.
  - Margin 3px, so a curve merely grazing a border is not counted.

THE ENGINE ALREADY HAS THE MACHINERY, which is what makes this a bug rather than
a missing feature. fm-layout has an obstacle spatial index (ObstacleSpatialIndex,
with the adaptive cell sizing from bd-1f8a35c) and nudge helpers
find_obstacle_nudge_x / find_obstacle_nudge_y. So obstacle avoidance exists and
is either not consulted on the routing path these edges take, or consulted and
then overridden. Establish WHICH before writing a fix -- the two have different
repairs and the wrong one will look like it works on these fixtures.

NOTE THE CONCENTRATION: 27 of 30 are in cycle_* fixtures, i.e. edges that were
REVERSED by cycle removal or that span non-adjacent ranks. That is a strong hint
about where to look, and also a warning that a fix tested only on acyclic
flowcharts will not exercise the failing path at all.

NEGATIVE CASES a naive implementation fails:
  1. The count must go DOWN without any edge changing endpoints. Assert per
     fixture that every edge still connects the same (source, target) pair -- a
     "fix" that reroutes by retargeting is not a fix.
  2. Node boxes must not move. This is an edge-routing bead; if node positions
     change, the layout checksum moves for reasons unrelated to the claim and
     the golden diff becomes unreadable. Assert node bounds byte-identical.
  3. Do not trade crossings for length: record total_edge_length before and
     after and state the change rather than hiding it. A router that avoids
     every node by taking enormous detours is worse, not better.
  4. The acyclic fixtures (flowchart_simple, all_edge_types, dense_flowchart_
     stress) currently have ZERO such crossings and must still have zero -- they
     are the control proving the fix did not perturb the common path.
  5. The probe itself needs its own control: run it against a fixture with a
     deliberately known crossing and confirm it reports it, so a drop to zero
     means "fixed" and not "probe broke".

GOLDEN EXPOSURE: fixing this WILL move cycle_braid, cycle_feedback, cycle_ladder,
cycle_scc_heavy and state_composite goldens plus their layout checksums. Bless
with a semantic diff, not a regeneration.
close_reason: Fixed: force_build_edge_paths now routes around obstacles. Test force_layout_edges_do_not_cross_unrelated_nodes with a non-vacuity control and an endpoint control; mechanism control confirms it fails without the fix. Gate: fm-layout 503 passed 0 failed; clippy -D warnings clean. See commit.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MECHANISM INVESTIGATION: two candidates RULED OUT, one strong lead, and one contradiction I could not resolve by reading. Recording it all so the next person does not repeat the dead ends.

THE AVOIDANCE MACHINERY IS WIRED IN AND DEMONSTRABLY WORKS. build_edge_paths (fm-layout lib.rs:14684) builds the obstacle set from ALL node bounds once, parks the current edge's own two endpoints at 1e30 so the AABB check rejects them, and passes the set to route_edge_points_with_obstacle_index for every non-self-loop edge. So this is not 'obstacle avoidance was never hooked up'.

MINIMAL REPRO PROVING IT WORKS, flowchart LR with L1 -> R1 plus a middle node R2:
  L1 x 92..192, R2 x 312..412, R1 x 532..632, all y 106..172.50
  edge 0 (L1 -> R1): M192 133.25 C 192 92 / C 277 92, 447 92, 532 92 / C 532 133.25
  edge 1 (R1 -> L1): same shape at y 104
Both detour ABOVE the node row (y 92 and 104, the row starts at 106) and neither touches R2. The nudge fired, produced a four-point staircase, and the renderer smoothed it. So the failing cases are NOT the generic path.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT IN THE FAILING CASES: the rows are not exactly aligned. In the repro all three nodes share y EXACTLY, so |source.y - target.y| < epsilon (0.001) takes the ALIGNED branch, which nudges in y. In cycle_ladder the boxes are L1 y=393.41, R2 y=393.41, R1 y=384.07 -- R1 sits 9.34px higher -- so the same edge takes the ELSE branch, which nudges a VERTICAL mid-segment in x instead.

THE CONTRADICTION, and it is the useful part. cycle_ladder edge 8 (L1 -> R1) is emitted as:
    M216.68 424.72 L356.68 419.27
TWO points, a straight line, straight through R2 (x 236.68..336.68, y 393.41..459.91) to a depth of 29.3px.

But NO branch of route_edge_points_with_obstacle_index can return two points here:
  - the |dy| < eps branch needs dy < 0.001; measured dy = 5.45
  - the |dx| < eps branch needs dx < 0.001; measured dx = 140
  - the else branch emits FOUR points whether or not the nudge fires -- with a nudge it is
    source,(nudge,sy),(nudge,ty),target and without one it is source,(mid_x,sy),(mid_x,ty),target
  - simplify_polyline cannot collapse either four-point form: it only drops AXIS-ALIGNED-COLLINEAR
    middles at epsilon 0.001, and (216.68,424.72),(286.68,424.72),(286.68,419.27) is neither
    x-collinear nor y-collinear.

So the two-point path was NOT produced by the router. Something between build_edge_paths and the emitted SVG is REPLACING the routed path with a direct line, discarding the avoidance that was already computed.

RULED OUT so far:
  - bundle_parallel_edges: groups by (source, target, arrow) which is ORDERED, so L1->R1 and
    R1->L1 land in different groups and neither reaches the min_bundle of 2.
  - simplify_polyline: shown above, cannot collapse the four-point forms.

STILL SUSPECT, in priority order:
  1. apply_parallel_offset. It runs AFTER routing (lib.rs:14799) and mutates the points in place with
     no re-check against obstacles. L1 and R1 ARE counted as a parallel pair here because
     edge_pair_count keys on (min(source,target), max(source,target)) -- UNORDERED -- so opposite-
     direction edges between the same two nodes are treated as parallel. Note the anchors are offset
     from the box centres by -1.94 and +1.95, consistent with an offset having been applied.
     Against this hypothesis: the minimal repro's edges 0/1 are also such a pair and kept four points.
  2. A renderer-side path rewrite. Not yet examined.

NEXT STEP, and it needs instrumentation rather than more reading: dump LayoutEdgePath.points for
cycle_ladder edge 8 straight out of build_edge_paths and compare with the emitted d= attribute. If
layout already holds two points the fault is in layout after routing; if it holds four the fault is
in the renderer. I did not guess between them -- a geometry mechanism asserted from reading rather
than confirmed by prediction is how this codebase has been burned before.
